items.summary: Reading time: 14 min The latest Amped FIVE update helps you spend less time troubleshooting CCTV footage and more time analyzing evidence. Access video from two popular encrypted formats, examine MP4 container issues, and handle changing video resolutions. Improved annotation and project tools also make it easier to prepare and present your findings. Hi everyone. It’s that time again, another Amped FIVE Update. CCTV and Forensic Video and Image analysis is hard enough; you don’t need to be battling challenges and bugs whilst working on an important investigation. With that in mind, over the past few months our developers have been working through many of your feature requests to improve the application and make your lives easier. Let’s take a quick look at what we have in store for you in this release. See the New Features in Action Key Takeaways Access more CCTV evidence : Decode video and extract timing data from Backup Player recordings, and decrypt supported password-protected Hikvision exports when you have the password. Investigate MP4 file issues : Use the new Atom Viewer to examine MP4 container structures, identify missing atoms, and recognize proprietary files disguised with an MP4 extension. Handle changing video resolutions : Segment CCTV streams when frame size changes so you can process different sections individually. Improve annotations and calibration : Create Bezier curves for more flexible annotations and use asymmetric circle patterns when calibrating cameras with challenging footage. Manage complex projects more efficiently : Export individual filter chains as standalone projects, deactivate unnecessary chains, and save minimal projects to reduce loading times. Improve traceability : Access original file information for timestamps and audio, and benefit from additional metadata in exported video and audio files. Formats The big news here is the decryption of two popular formats. The first change comes in the decoding of the video contained within this type of executable. Backup Player Source: Google https://jp.images-monotaro.com/etc/pdf/manual/manual_50995904_20231205_01.pdf It’s usually referred to as Backup Player, but could have many different names and also different interfaces or color schemes. The format team here at Amped Towers has been hard at work to enable full decoding of this video type, including full extraction of all the timing data. The imagery is no longer locked inside the player, allowing easy and forensic analysis of the video. The next change comes in the form of the password-protected Hikvision formats that use the MP4 extension (but are not ISO MP4 Standard). Hikvision IMKH These proprietary formats can be confusing as they use a standard extension. We will look more at this a little later with another exciting addition to Advanced File Info . Individual CCTV systems can be set to export encrypted data, which then requires a password to decrypt and play. In this latest release, we have added the capability to automatically read a password file within Convert DVR . If a password file is not there when Convert DVR attempts to extract the data, then you will see this message. Simply create a standard text file containing the password, rename it using the naming convention of . .password. Convert DVR will see it, use it…and decrypt the video. Here is a directory with a password file. In future releases, the password entry will be simplified. For now, we wanted to make this capability available to you without delay. After the conversion process completes, you will receive a decrypted file, along with your Stream Copied, newly formatted file. Although the functionality for using passwords is now built-in, it is often best to ensure that native exports do not have encryption to start with. Passwords can get lost, and in many cases with other systems, they can restrict your analysis of the video. Along with those new developments, we have also added several more proprietary formats, enabling you to decode the video and extract the timing data from those pesky CCTV files. Thank you to everyone who has submitted files for analysis and support to the codec team. With your help, we learned that these proprietary formats exist. Developing the forensic demuxers, extractors, and decoders helps everyone within the forensic video community. Let’s move on from the formats and look at the new additions in FIVE. Advanced File Info Do you remember earlier we mentioned the MP4 Container format? The new addition here is the Atom Viewer, designed to analyze the MP4 format. The MP4 Container Format is very common. It is structured with individual Atoms that contain the data. For example, in the image above, we have highlighted an Edit List Box in the Video Track. It’s possible to identify that there is an Edit List duration of 66ms. This may help explain why 2 frames (2 x 33ms duration) are not displayed at the start of the MP4, but can be displayed if the stream is placed in a different container. Knowing container structures is vital for quickly answering questions when things don’t work, or unexpected events happen. You may receive several MP4 files, but one fails to decode. A common problem is that this Atom, the “MOOV”, is missing. In the image below, we can see this important Atom. It contains all the instructions on how to decode the video frames. If there was an issue at the end of the recording, it’s possible that the “MOOV” would fail to be written. Quickly identifying this issue could help you. What about this file? It has an MP4 file extension, but no Atom tree is displayed. It is not in the MP4 format. It is a proprietary format, and some of you will recognise that header in the ASCII text. Yes, it’s a Hikvision file like the one we looked at earlier. If you want to learn more about containers and formats, consider signing up for the training modules . Also, check out our blog series on formats and conversion if you’d like to explore this topic further. Convert DVR We are always looking at how to help you in the initial stages of an investigation when you are preparing the video for analysis. Convert DVR is often required, not only for proprietary formats, but for standard ones with some “challenges”. One such challenge is CCTV video streams that change their resolution. It’s usually triggered when motion is detected, and here we have a video stream where exactly this has happened. At frame 3397, the resolution jumps from 640×378 to 2688×1594. This means that the two parts need to be processed differently. So, how do we segment this file? Under the Advanced tab of Convert DVR , you will now find an option to Segment on frame size changes. This works on proprietary formats and on timing data as well. You can now decide which segments are of interest and then process those according to what is required. Before we move on, there is another small update to Convert DVR within the Fallback Procedures options. We have added the WAV container format as an option within custom commands to enable audio-only output. Annotate There is never an update without a new addition to Annotate . When using the Arrow/Line tool, you can now apply a Bezier curve. It’s very easy to control the points and get the desired result. In other Annotate news, we have also added two more duration control options under the Right-click functionality. These make setting your Annotate ranges so much easier. And finally, you may notice a small change to the Magnify control options. We have simplified the selection of either controlling the Source Area or the Magnify Area. Camera Calibration The Camera Calibration filter gets a new pattern! “Asymmetric Circles” may be preferred in some circumstances. It may be difficult to get the checkerboard corners in highly compressed video, but visualizing the circles is easier. The width and height are calculated by the rows and columns, but it’s important to know that 2 columns are considered in the count. This is a 6×6 pattern. You will also notice another very handy button at the bottom of the filter pattern tab. You can now save a PDF of the pattern to be used. Ideal for printing out. There have also been two other smaller improvements: Added a checkbox for zero tangential distortion within the Calibration Model tab. This then assumes that the lens is exactly parallel with the image plane. Moved the Show Live Points checkbox to the output tab and renamed it to Show Detected Points. Interlacing We now have several updates relating to the deinterlacing of footage. Even after many years of video being “born digital”, there are still many analog-based systems that retain the signal fields. The first change is in the Inspector tool. After using the Deinterlace filter, the field being shown will be presented in the Details. The second change is in the Player bar. This will again show you what field is being displayed. We move now to the third change, and this is within the Macros that can be used in Add Text and Annotate. You can now use this field type data as viewable information using the new $FIELDTYPE Macro. Video Writer and Audio Writer In this release, we have added metadata to all video and audio exported using both writer filters. After writing a file, the information about the application and writing method is added to the file’s metadata. In the image above, we have a video file that was written using Amped FIVE rev. 42534, and the writing method was High. History The History Panel also gets some updates for this release. There are many situations where you have a large project but then require a single chain to be handled differently. Under the chains’ right-click options, you now have the ability to save only that chain as a standalone project. This creates a much smaller project that may be much more suitable for sharing or further work. Important note : Link filters and their associated chains are not yet able to be exported as a standalone project. This will come in a future release. Following on from this, we now have the ability to activate and deactivate all the filters in a chain. You may have a large project and need to deactivate some filter chains to allow faster loading next time you open the project. Before we get to another update that can help with making projects a bit lighter, we have another History change. In the View tab, you can now lock the tabs to the same order as your filter chains. This makes navigating much easier, as your viewer tabs are in the same order as your filter chains. Projects In the last section, we presented some new functions to deactivate and activate all the filters in a chain. The result is that these chains then do not get automatically loaded when the project is opened. This release brings another update to help here. Save Minimal Project saves every folder, chain, and filter, but deactivates everything that is not required for the project to be opened. This can save a huge amount of time when dealing with multiple chains of many filters. Original File When a file is loaded, and FIVE detects that there is data that needs extracting or converting, the Convert DVR utility takes over. The result is that you may end up with several new and different files. For video, there has always been an extra tab within the loader detailing where this new video originated from. That’s the Original File. For both Load Timestamp and Load Audio , this Original File tab now appears in the filter settings too. In the image above, we have the timestamp created after a conversion from a DAV file. The file it originated from is now logged within the filter. Load Subtitle If a subtitle contains just date and time information, it is usually detected and loaded directly as a timestamp with the Load Timestamp filter. There are, however, many CCTV export systems that export their metadata and date and time information all together. This means there is other information, perhaps location or camera name. This data then gets loaded automatically by FIVE using the Load Subtitle filter. What happens if you want to use the date and time information within that file to control the video speed, for instance? Within the filter, you will now find a button to load this file as a timestamp. The Load Subtitle filter will be disabled, and the file will be loaded as a timestamp. You can then add in any bespoke input format and use the data for video timing. If you need to display the subtitle data on the screen, then it’s easily re-enabled. Time Calculator Staying on the “time” theme, we have made a small change to the Time Calculator tool. You no longer have to manually add .000 at the end if the time values you are calculating do not have milliseconds. They will be added automatically at the time of calculation. This makes it much easier to copy and paste from time sources that do not have milliseconds. Text Filters We have added a new background option to the text. This adds a small colored outline to the text. It’s a small but very significant improvement in contrast. And finally… Sequence Writer Image sequences are a very useful way of exporting visual multimedia. In this release, we have added an advanced rename functionality so you can create the filenames you require for your investigation. There we go, that’s all the major updates and changes covered. Before we go, let us look at some important library updates, smaller changes, and the all-important bug fixes. Library Updates The following library packages have been updated in this release: FFmpeg library to version 8.1 Libheif library to version 1.23.5. De265 library to version 1.1.3. Other Updates and Changes Here are some other smaller improvements and changes in this release. Installer: it’s now possible to skip or postpone the installation of files in the Documents folder, thus allowing you to complete the installation on setups having the Documents folder on a network path. System log file names now contain a “system” suffix after the datetime. Video files with an audio extension can now be directly loaded without conversion. Improved the extraction of subtitle streams. A pop-up message is now displayed when processing filters outside canvas bounds. Date format can now include forward slashes. Improved the presentation of the Filter panel contents when adjusting the panel’s width. Blank Video : now parses PTS data to allow linking with other chains. Removed file path dependency from the Hash filter. The QuickTime and USBPlay Video Engines have been removed from Video Loader as now redundant. Convert Frame Rate : improved the filter help description. Bookmarks panel: improved the separation between the bookmarks list and the description text. Hide Selection : added support for preset and assistant script functions for this filter. Enabled the system’s spell checker in the Bookmarks Description pop-up window. Filter parameters: removed trailing zeros from decimals in spin controls. Filter parameters: improved the handling of slider values when not matching the parameter step. Adjust Timestamp : added the ability to set the save location when exporting the adjusted timestamp file. Improved the layout of message dialogs with very long text by adding word wrapping. Added support for line breaks in the bookmark Description text within the report. Video Mixer : added the “Clear Input Delay” button. Bug Fixes Thanks to all the users who have reported bugs. They can be annoying, so if you find one, please reach out to us in support so we can fix it. Fixed a bug in Convert Frame Rate causing the last frame to be dropped while increasing the frame rate of a clip. Fixed a bug with Copy & Verify stopping calculation of hashes after one file has failed to copy. Fixed an issue causing a filter to deactivate when moving chains. Fixed an issue with the Assistant panel color theme. Fixed an issue with ARP Replay projects containing a Resize filter not loading correctly. Fixed a bug in Annotate that prevented the Annotate-Text “Padding” feature from working properly. Fixed an issue in Annotate causing an Annotate object to extend when the Loop mode is activated in the Player Panel. Fixed a bug causing the text position to be wrongly moved when navigating out of a keyframe in Annotate . Fixed a bug with the Audio Writer Sample Rate. Fixed a bug causing the overwrite existing files parameter to be ignored while using fallback recipes in Convert DVR. Fixed a bug causing the Correct Fisheye filter to produce distorted output due to insufficient Focal Length precision. Fixed a bug causing a bookmark description to be cut off if the text is too long. Fixed a bug causing the description of the filter to be only partially shown. Fixed a bug causing a crash when duplicating a chain and replacing the input file in a loader filter. Fixed a bug causing a misalignment of the Player bar and Audio Waveform. Fixed a bug causing the Size slider to flicker. Fixed a bug in Range Selector causing the program to crash if the step parameter is set to 0. Fixed a bug that allowed the user to set negative values in the Frame parameter within Single Selector . Fixed a bug occasionally causing a non-deterministic audio-video mux output. Fixed a bug that caused the software to crash when adding the Milestone Client filter. Fixed a bug causing the Batch Convert DVR dialog to appear incorrectly while loading multi-stream .image files. Fixed a bug causing a crash to the desktop when using the Freeze Frame filter in conjunction with a Link filter. Fixed a bug causing the installer to fail on FIPS-enabled systems. Fixed a bug in Multiview that could cause a crash after deleting and re-adding a filter affecting the source inputs. Don’t Delay – Update Today If you have an active support plan, you can update straight away by going into the menu About > Check for Updates within Amped FIVE. If you need to renew your SMS plan, please contact us or one of our authorized partners. And remember that you can always manage your license and requests from the Amped Support Portal . FAQ – Amped FIVE Update 42578 Can Amped FIVE decode encrypted CCTV video files? Yes. The latest FIVE update adds support for decoding video from Backup Player executable files and decrypting supported password-protected Hikvision formats with an MP4 extension. You can access the video for forensic analysis, including extracting timing information, instead of relying solely on proprietary players. How can I decrypt password-protected Hikvision video files in Amped FIVE? You can decrypt supported Hikvision video exports using Convert DVR. Create a text file containing the correct password and name it ..password. Convert DVR automatically detects the password file and uses it during conversion. How can I identify problems with an MP4 video file? You can use the new Atom Viewer in Advanced File Info to inspect the internal structure of MP4 containers. This helps you identify issues such as a missing MOOV atom, examine edit lists that may affect frame presentation, and recognize proprietary formats using an MP4 extension. What’s new for video annotations and camera calibration in Amped FIVE? You can now create Bezier curves with the Arrow/Line tool for more flexible annotations. Camera Calibration also supports asymmetric circle patterns, which may be easier to detect than checkerboard corners in highly compressed footage. You can also export calibration patterns as printable PDFs. How can I process CCTV footage that changes resolution during recording? In Convert DVR, enable the new “Segment on frame size changes” option under the Advanced tab. This allows you to split video streams when their resolution changes, so you can select and process individual segments according to your analysis requirements. How can I manage large Amped FIVE projects more efficiently? You can use Save Minimal Project to deactivate components that aren’t required when opening a project, potentially reducing loading times. You can also save individual filter chains as standalone projects, although chains involving Link filters cannot yet be exported independently. How does Amped FIVE help maintain traceability during forensic video analysis? The Original File information is now available in the Load Timestamp and Load Audio filters, helping you trace extracted data back to its source. Video Writer and Audio Writer also add information about the application and writing method to exported files’ metadata. https://blog.ampedsoftware.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/FIVE-update-42578-1.png

Bug Fixes

Thanks to all the users who have reported bugs. They can be annoying, so if you find one, please reach out to us in support so we can fix it.

  • Fixed a bug in Convert Frame Rate causing the last frame to be dropped while increasing the frame rate of a clip. Fixed a bug with Copy & Verify stopping calculation of hashes after one file has failed to copy.
  • Fixed an issue causing a filter to deactivate when moving chains.
  • Fixed an issue with the Assistant panel color theme.
  • Fixed an issue with ARP Replay projects containing a Resize filter not loading correctly.
  • Fixed a bug in Annotate that prevented the Annotate-Text “Padding” feature from working properly.
  • Fixed an issue in Annotate causing an Annotate object to extend when the Loop mode is activated in the Player Panel.
  • Fixed a bug causing the text position to be wrongly moved when navigating out of a keyframe in Annotate.
  • Fixed a bug with the Audio Writer Sample Rate.
  • Fixed a bug causing the overwrite existing files parameter to be ignored while using fallback recipes in Convert DVR.
  • Fixed a bug causing the Correct Fisheye filter to produce distorted output due to insufficient Focal Length precision.
  • Fixed a bug causing a bookmark description to be cut off if the text is too long.
  • Fixed a bug causing the description of the filter to be only partially shown.
  • Fixed a bug causing a crash when duplicating a chain and replacing the input file in a loader filter.
  • Fixed a bug causing a misalignment of the Player bar and Audio Waveform.
  • Fixed a bug causing the Size slider to flicker.
  • Fixed a bug in Range Selector causing the program to crash if the step parameter is set to 0.
  • Fixed a bug that allowed the user to set negative values in the Frame parameter within Single Selector.
  • Fixed a bug occasionally causing a non-deterministic audio-video mux output.
  • Fixed a bug that caused the software to crash when adding the Milestone Client filter.
  • Fixed a bug causing the Batch Convert DVR dialog to appear incorrectly while loading multi-stream .image files.
  • Fixed a bug causing a crash to the desktop when using the Freeze Frame filter in conjunction with a Link filter.
  • Fixed a bug causing the installer to fail on FIPS-enabled systems.
  • Fixed a bug in Multiview that could cause a crash after deleting and re-adding a filter affecting the source inputs.

Don’t Delay – Update Today

If you have an active support plan, you can update straight away by going into the menu About > Check for Updates within Amped FIVE. If you need to renew your SMS plan, please contact us or one of our authorized partners. And remember that you can always manage your license and requests from the Amped Support Portal.

FAQ – Amped FIVE Update 42578

Can Amped FIVE decode encrypted CCTV video files?

Yes. The latest FIVE update adds support for decoding video from Backup Player executable files and decrypting supported password-protected Hikvision formats with an MP4 extension. You can access the video for forensic analysis, including extracting timing information, instead of relying solely on proprietary players.

How can I decrypt password-protected Hikvision video files in Amped FIVE?

You can decrypt supported Hikvision video exports using Convert DVR. Create a text file containing the correct password and name it ..password. Convert DVR automatically detects the password file and uses it during conversion.

How can I identify problems with an MP4 video file?

You can use the new Atom Viewer in Advanced File Info to inspect the internal structure of MP4 containers. This helps you identify issues such as a missing MOOV atom, examine edit lists that may affect frame presentation, and recognize proprietary formats using an MP4 extension.

What’s new for video annotations and camera calibration in Amped FIVE?

You can now create Bezier curves with the Arrow/Line tool for more flexible annotations. Camera Calibration also supports asymmetric circle patterns, which may be easier to detect than checkerboard corners in highly compressed footage. You can also export calibration patterns as printable PDFs.

How can I process CCTV footage that changes resolution during recording?

In Convert DVR, enable the new “Segment on frame size changes” option under the Advanced tab. This allows you to split video streams when their resolution changes, so you can select and process individual segments according to your analysis requirements.

How can I manage large Amped FIVE projects more efficiently?

You can use Save Minimal Project to deactivate components that aren’t required when opening a project, potentially reducing loading times. You can also save individual filter chains as standalone projects, although chains involving Link filters cannot yet be exported independently.

How does Amped FIVE help maintain traceability during forensic video analysis?

The Original File information is now available in the Load Timestamp and Load Audio filters, helping you trace extracted data back to its source. Video Writer and Audio Writer also add information about the application and writing method to exported files’ metadata.

items.title: Report: 9 out of 10 Americans Have Been Targeted by Scams
items.summary: 91% of Americans have been targeted by a scam, and 17% have fallen victim to one, according to a new survey by Consumer Reports. Notably, 20% of respondents said the latest scam they encountered was personalized, indicating that attackers are increasingly using automation and public or leaked information to craft targeted phishing attacks.

items.title: Cloudflare and OpenAI: making AI discovery better for everyone
items.summary: Optimizing your site for AI is of little use if AI can't find it. The answer to someone's question may already be on your website: the installation guide you spent a week writing, or a first-hand account of using a product, with the details that make the difference for whether they buy it. As more people turn to AI for help, you want those systems to find your work, represent it accurately, and send interested people your way. You also want control over how they access your site. Cloudflare and OpenAI launched a research pilot in July 2026 with those interests in mind. We wanted to find out whether signals from Cloudflare’s network could help ChatGPT users discover new content more efficiently. Today, we’re sharing early results. So far, the answer is a resounding yes: the pilot has brought previously unknown pages into OpenAI’s search index, giving ChatGPT more sources to draw on to help people find relevant, timely information. Along the way, we’ve learned more about what makes a page worth discovering and how AI systems use the web. Finding more of the web The web is full of specifics. Someone fixing a washing machine needs the manual for their exact model. Someone applying for a passport needs the current requirements and fees. Someone choosing a local restaurant needs its latest menu and opening hours. Finding the right page can be the difference between a wrong answer and one that actually helps. These pages can be valuable even if few other sites link to them. In the previous version of the web, discoverability was getting to the top of a search result page. It was then up to the human who visited your page to determine the value of the information, book that table, apply for that passport. As people increasingly rely on AI to find information and complete tasks, discoverability matters in new ways. AI systems need to find the right sources, understand what's useful, and connect people with relevant information – whether that's through an answer, a citation, or a visit to the website itself. Cloudflare's network provides signals that can help OpenAI’s search crawler discover more useful pages across the web to surface to ChatGPT users. OpenAI then independently evaluates and ranks how those pages appear based on how relevant and helpful they are. Together, this creates a feedback loop that can improve both discovery and the quality of information people find. This joint pilot, which used a participating cohort of ~1% of Cloudflare’s total network, has enabled OpenAI to discover and index hundreds of millions of new web pages, helping people discover more useful content and get more questions answered through ChatGPT. By linking back to relevant sources, ChatGPT Search also gives people a way to explore the original content and discover the websites and publishers behind it. With GPT-6 and Intelligent UI , OpenAI is also making ChatGPT an even better place to shop, learn, and find answers, with more visual, interactive experiences tailored to what people need. This work complements these advances by helping ChatGPT discover more useful, up-to-date information from across the web. From discovery to useful answers Finding a URL is only the start. We need to know whether it leads to a page someone can access, whether that page offers anything distinct, and what it might help someone do. We’ve learned, for example, how easily automated traffic can make a nonexistent page look interesting. Bots repeatedly ask for files that aren’t there. Some sites redirect almost any address to their homepage. Other addresses lead to copies of the same content. Recognizing these patterns gives us a way to cut wasted work before a crawler fetches the page, and improve efficiency in a way that benefits site owners. We're also testing signals that identify and flag potentially harmful pages, adding another layer of information to support safer, more reliable discovery. A legitimate site can have a single compromised page, such as a fake login form planted by an attacker. Flagging that one page, rather than the whole domain, keeps people safe without penalizing the site owner. Early results suggest these signals can help identify pages that should be kept out of an index. Making discovery easier As more people use AI to discover information, website owners have new opportunities to reach interested audiences. For those who choose to make their content available to AI systems, these improvements make discovery easier and more efficient. Keeping up by fetching every page more often would be expensive for everyone. For a website owner, a crawler that repeatedly downloads an unchanged page adds load without bringing any benefit. The signals above are how we avoid that. Filtering keeps crawlers away from pages that don't exist or that redirect elsewhere. Change signals tell them when a page is worth another visit, and when it isn't. There's a balance to get right. Finding new pages can initially increase crawling as those pages are evaluated and indexed. The goal is to keep discovering and stay current while reducing the work that takes. For Cloudflare customers, that means less unnecessary load. For OpenAI, it means more of its search resources are spent on information that helps people. Making it worthwhile to participate The next phase will build on what we’ve learned: improve the selection of pages, test faster and more reliable change signals, and measure what happens after content is discovered. We’re continuing to work with OpenAI to understand how better site discovery can translate into real business outcomes, and we’ll keep sharing what we learn along the way. Domain owners’ choices matter throughout. A signal about a page doesn’t grant permission to access it. This research uses metadata about the web for search and discovery, rather than sharing page content for model training. You can use Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control to understand and manage how AI systems access your website.

  • You missed a package delivery 
  • There’s a problem with your bank account 
  • You need to reset a password or verify your identity 
  • You owe a toll, fine, or other payment 
  • You’ve won a prize or are eligible for a refund 
How to check if a link is safe 

Using Malwarebytes Scam Link Check is simple and takes just a few steps: 

  1. Copy the suspicious link without opening it. 
  2. Paste the link into the tool.  
  3. Wait while Malwarebytes scans the site for potential threats. 
  4. Review the results.  

If we can’t determine whether a link is safe, it’s best not to click it yet. Instead, reach out to the company using the contact details listed on its official website.

Scammers are getting more adept at creating convincing copies of a brand’s site, making it even harder to decipher what’s real and what’s not.

items.title: UK Legal Aid Agency Data Breach Exposes Personal Records Dating Back to 1978
items.summary: The UK Legal Aid Agency (LAA) has confirmed that its 2025 cyberattack stole personal records dating back to 1978. An updated investigation found approximately 250,000 records from before 2007, widening the known scope of a breach that affected legal aid applicants, providers and some probation service users. In its October 14, 2026 update , the agency said most affected data concerned applications, claims, payments or cases active between January 2007 and May 16, 2025. Most older records came from the 1990s and 2000s, with very few dating from before 1990. The LAA first detected the attack on April 23, 2025, and warned legal aid providers that information, including financial details, might have been compromised. On May 16, investigators established that attackers had accessed and stolen a significant amount of personal data, making the incident more serious than initially understood. Technical teams have since examined data spread across several complex systems. Much of the material was unstructured, split into separate parts or left incomplete, making it hard to determine exactly what attackers took. The latest findings reflect further analysis of the original incident rather than a newly disclosed attack. Personal, Financial and Court Records Affected Depending on the person and case, stolen information may include names, addresses, dates of birth, National Insurance numbers, financial assessments and legal case details. Some Crown Court records contain charges, pleas, convictions and sentences. Other records may include information about partners, family members and parties involved in civil proceedings. The oldest category includes benefit checks linked to civil legal aid between 1978 and 2012. Provider information may include bank account names, account numbers, sort codes, payment records and online portal user details. However, the agency stressed that neither every person nor every listed data field was necessarily affected. The breach also highlights the sensitivity of court information, an issue seen in the separate NSW Online Registry data breach , where approximately 9,000 court documents were downloaded without permission. That incident is not linked to the LAA attack. Investigators also found probation data belonging to a relatively small number of people supervised between 2010 and 2017. More than 99% related to supervision during 2016 and 2017. Exposed fields included some names, birth dates, nationalities and case references. The agency said this probation data did not concern crime victims. The LAA says it has no indication that stolen information has been published or shared. Its update does not identify the attackers or explain their entry method. Security work includes stronger authentication, tighter access controls, better monitoring, vulnerability fixes, and isolating or retiring higher-risk technology. Such measures also involve patch management practices People who believe they may be affected should watch for unexpected messages and independently verify requests for personal or financial information. The NCSC’s data breach guidance recommends contacting organizations through official channels, avoiding contact details supplied in suspicious messages, replacing reused passwords, and checking accounts for unusual activity following a breach. items.title: KGB RAT Malware Bypasses Windows Defender to Steal Credentials and Control PCs
items.summary: A Windows remote access trojan called KGB RAT gives attackers a way to spy on infected computers, collect credentials and control a victim’s desktop. The malware is sold as a service and advertised with a “fully undetectable” crypter that its sellers claim can bypass Windows Defender and other antivirus products. That claim should be treated carefully: Group-IB’s report documents the advertised evasion and observed malicious behavior, but does not show that every version can reliably defeat Defender on every system. Analysts and researchers from Group-IB identified and analyzed KGB RAT, finding a tool that combines credential theft, keylogging, remote control and ransomware features. The researchers also found that its operators use a separate Telegram channel to receive infection alerts, while the malware contacts command-and-control (C2) servers for instructions. KGB RAT Malware Bypasses Windows Defender Group-IB said KGB RAT was promoted on underground forums from late 2025, but traces of an early version of its server infrastructure date to January 2022. The malware is sold through a malware-as-a-service model, meaning buyers can rent access rather than build their own tool. The seller advertises daily crypter updates and a payload builder that can create files in formats including EXE, BAT, HTA and REG. The product is presented as a legitimate remote administration tool. Its advertised features include file access, webcam and microphone control, password recovery, hidden desktop access and tools for managing multiple infected computers. Group-IB’s analysis found samples based on an obfuscated version of NjRAT, a known remote access trojan. This connection matters because KGB RAT is not simply a new name: it builds on existing malware code and adds a commercial package around it. KGB RAT key features (Source – Group-IB) The report also shows why a RAT can be dangerous even when it does not use a new technique. A related NjRAT campaign abusing Microsoft Dev Tunnels shows how familiar malware can use trusted online services to hide its network traffic. KGB RAT takes a different route, using Telegram for alerts and direct C2 connections for remote control. In Group-IB’s tested sample, the original program copied itself into a temporary folder and relaunched as svchost.exe , a name that resembles a real Windows process. It then created a scheduled task called ChromeUpdate to run again when a user signs in. The malware also changed a Windows setting that controls the display of hidden system files and modified a setting related to security-zone warnings. The malware checks the computer before carrying out its work. Group-IB observed it querying Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for information about the operating system, running processes and installed security products. It also checked for signs of virtual machines and analysis tools. These steps can help malware avoid running in a research sandbox or reveal which defenses are present. How KGB RAT takes hold and stays active For credential theft, researchers observed the sample accessing Windows Credential Manager files. These can hold saved sign-in details for websites, network resources and applications. KGB RAT also includes a keylogger that can record keyboard activity, as well as features for screenshots, clipboard monitoring and remote desktop control. Its hidden VNC feature is designed to give an operator a remote view or control session that may not be visible on the victim’s desktop. Readers can learn more about this method in Cybersecurity News’ article on hidden VNC remote desktop control . Group-IB observed the malware looking up a victim’s public IP address through ip-api.com and sending an infection notification through Telegram’s Bot API. KGB RAT website sells the malware as a professional system administrator tool (Source – Group-IB) The report also describes a Crypto Clipper feature in one analyzed sample. This type of tool watches copied cryptocurrency addresses and may replace them with an address controlled by the attacker. KGB RAT’s sellers claim its crypter can bypass or disable Windows Defender. A crypter changes or wraps malware code to make it harder for antivirus products to recognize a file by its signature. The seller’s claim is not proof that all builds evade protection. Group-IB says its own Malware Detonation Platform detected samples by observing their behavior, including after obfuscation or unpacking. That distinction is useful for defenders: a file may change, but its actions can still raise alarms. In the analyzed sample, warning signs included a program running from a temporary folder, an unfamiliar ChromeUpdate task, registry changes, suspicious child processes and connections to Telegram or the listed C2 servers. A Cybersecurity News report on Silver RAT antivirus bypass methods provides further context on how RAT sellers use crypters and other evasion claims. Organizations should keep endpoint protection active and updated, restrict unapproved software, and alert on scheduled tasks created by programs running from user-writable folders. Security teams should review unusual process chains and outbound connections, especially when Telegram or the listed geolocation service is contacted by a non-browser process. If infection is suspected, isolate the device, preserve logs and investigate from a clean system before resetting exposed credentials and sessions. items.summary_html:
A Windows remote access trojan called KGB RAT gives attackers a way to spy on infected computers, collect credentials and control a victim’s desktop.

The malware is sold as a service and advertised with a “fully undetectable” crypter that its sellers claim can bypass Windows Defender and other antivirus products.

That claim should be treated carefully: Group-IB’s report documents the advertised evasion and observed malicious behavior, but does not show that every version can reliably defeat Defender on every system.

Analysts and researchers from Group-IB identified and analyzed KGB RAT, finding a tool that combines credential theft, keylogging, remote control and ransomware features.

The researchers also found that its operators use a separate Telegram channel to receive infection alerts, while the malware contacts command-and-control (C2) servers for instructions.

KGB RAT Malware Bypasses Windows Defender

Group-IB said KGB RAT was promoted on underground forums from late 2025, but traces of an early version of its server infrastructure date to January 2022.

The malware is sold through a malware-as-a-service model, meaning buyers can rent access rather than build their own tool. The seller advertises daily crypter updates and a payload builder that can create files in formats including EXE, BAT, HTA and REG.

The product is presented as a legitimate remote administration tool. Its advertised features include file access, webcam and microphone control, password recovery, hidden desktop access and tools for managing multiple infected computers.

Group-IB’s analysis found samples based on an obfuscated version of NjRAT, a known remote access trojan. This connection matters because KGB RAT is not simply a new name: it builds on existing malware code and adds a commercial package around it.

KGB RAT key features (Source – Group-IB)

The report also shows why a RAT can be dangerous even when it does not use a new technique. A related NjRAT campaign abusing Microsoft Dev Tunnels shows how familiar malware can use trusted online services to hide its network traffic. KGB RAT takes a different route, using Telegram for alerts and direct C2 connections for remote control.

In Group-IB’s tested sample, the original program copied itself into a temporary folder and relaunched as svchost.exe, a name that resembles a real Windows process.

It then created a scheduled task called ChromeUpdate to run again when a user signs in. The malware also changed a Windows setting that controls the display of hidden system files and modified a setting related to security-zone warnings.

The malware checks the computer before carrying out its work. Group-IB observed it querying Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for information about the operating system, running processes and installed security products.

It also checked for signs of virtual machines and analysis tools. These steps can help malware avoid running in a research sandbox or reveal which defenses are present.

How KGB RAT takes hold and stays active

For credential theft, researchers observed the sample accessing Windows Credential Manager files. These can hold saved sign-in details for websites, network resources and applications.

KGB RAT also includes a keylogger that can record keyboard activity, as well as features for screenshots, clipboard monitoring and remote desktop control.

Its hidden VNC feature is designed to give an operator a remote view or control session that may not be visible on the victim’s desktop. Readers can learn more about this method in Cybersecurity News’ article on hidden VNC remote desktop control.

Group-IB observed the malware looking up a victim’s public IP address through ip-api.com and sending an infection notification through Telegram’s Bot API.

KGB RAT website sells the malware as a professional system administrator tool (Source – Group-IB)

The report also describes a Crypto Clipper feature in one analyzed sample. This type of tool watches copied cryptocurrency addresses and may replace them with an address controlled by the attacker.

KGB RAT’s sellers claim its crypter can bypass or disable Windows Defender. A crypter changes or wraps malware code to make it harder for antivirus products to recognize a file by its signature.

The seller’s claim is not proof that all builds evade protection. Group-IB says its own Malware Detonation Platform detected samples by observing their behavior, including after obfuscation or unpacking.

That distinction is useful for defenders: a file may change, but its actions can still raise alarms. In the analyzed sample, warning signs included a program running from a temporary folder, an unfamiliar ChromeUpdate task, registry changes, suspicious child processes and connections to Telegram or the listed C2 servers.

A Cybersecurity News report on Silver RAT antivirus bypass methods provides further context on how RAT sellers use crypters and other evasion claims.

Organizations should keep endpoint protection active and updated, restrict unapproved software, and alert on scheduled tasks created by programs running from user-writable folders.

Security teams should review unusual process chains and outbound connections, especially when Telegram or the listed geolocation service is contacted by a non-browser process.

If infection is suspected, isolate the device, preserve logs and investigate from a clean system before resetting exposed credentials and sessions.

items.title: Critical Next.js Vulnerabilities Allow Hackers to Execute Malicious Code Remotely
items.summary: Next.js has released security updates for two critical vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers run malicious code without logging in. A third, high-severity flaw could stop affected applications from serving requests. The issues involve cached functions, SVG image processing, and Server Actions, with fixes available in Next.js 16.4.1 and 15.5.28. Published on October 14, 2026, the advisories describe separate attack paths with different requirements Both remote code execution flaws score 9.5, while the denial-of-service issue scores 8.2. Application settings and enabled features determine exposure, so version checks are only one part of risk assessment. The first vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr, affects App Router applications using Cache Components. An application becomes vulnerable when a use cache function returns multiple typed arrays. Under these conditions, attackers could achieve remote code execution without authentication or user interaction. Next.js releases 16.0.0–16.4.0 are affected by the flaw, which is fixed in version 16.4.1. Developers should upgrade immediately, as no workaround or CVE identifier is available. Critical Next.js Vulnerabilities Earlier React and Next.js RCE reports highlight server-side risks , but the newly disclosed cache flaw has a separate trigger and is unrelated to React2Shell. The second flaw, CVE-2026-96889, involves a memory-related weakness in an upstream library the Image Optimization API uses to handle SVG files. It can lead to remote code execution on Next.js deployments running on glibc-based Linux. The advisory lists no required privileges or user interaction. The official image optimization advisory lists affected versions as 10.0.0 through 15.5.27 and versions above 16.0.0 through 16.4.0. Developers can address this issue by ensuring Next.js uses sharp 0.35.5 or later. Installing the patched Next.js releases ensures package managers provide a fixed dependency. The third vulnerability, GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r, affects App Router applications with at least one Server Action. Crafted requests can drive excessive CPU usage, preventing the same process from handling further requests. Applications using Pages Router, or those without Server Actions, are not vulnerable. Affected versions include 13.0.0 through 15.5.27 and 16.0.0 through 16.4.0. There is no workaround besides upgrading. Previous coverage of Next.js security patches highlights related feature-specific risks, but those earlier fixes do not replace this update. Developers should install Next.js 15.5.28 or 16.4.1 as appropriate. Updating only sharp addresses the image flaw, not the separate cached-function or Server Actions vulnerabilities. items.title: Turn Threat Reports into Behavior Rules in Minutes with AI
items.summary: Every day, threat intelligence teams read reports describing new attacker campaigns, and every day detection engineers face the same question: how do we turn this into detection content before the threat reaches our environment? Reading a long report, spotting the behaviors that matter, and writing a correct rule by hand takes time that most SOC teams don’t have. Prime Architect gives security teams a faster way to handle this. Prime Architect is SOC Prime’s AI-powered workspace for threat research and detection engineering. Its agentic tools analyze threat intelligence and produce actionable defense content, so security teams can move from raw reports to detections faster. A good place to start is generating behavior rules. Paste a threat report, and Prime Architect generates one or several behavior rules in Sigma format, ready to review, refine and deploy. Why Use AI to Generate a Behavior Rule? Behavior-based detections look for what attackers do rather than for indicators that change from one campaign to the next. They are more resilient and valuable, but also harder and slower to write. Using AI to generate a behavior rule removes the most time-consuming part of that work. Faster time to detection. Go from a fresh threat report to a draft rule in a single workflow instead of hours of manual analysis. Less manual effort. AI reads the report and extracts the behaviors worth detecting, so your engineers can focus on tuning and validation. Coverage from a single source. Depending on the context you provide, AI can generate one behavior rule or multiple behavior rules from the same report. Open, portable output. Rules are created as behavior rules in a Sigma format, so you can translate them into the language of your SIEM, EDR, or data lake. One continuous workflow. Generation is only the start. You can validate, summarize, translate, deploy, and refine the rule without leaving the platform. Contact Sales How to Generate a Behavior Rule Behavior Rule with AI is one of the agentic AI tools available in the Agentic Threat Research mode of Prime Architect. Here is how to use it: Open Prime Architect and go to the Agentic Threat Research mode. Click Code Editor in the upper right corner and paste the text of a threat report. Select the Generate button. Select the Behavior Rule tool from the agentic AI tools options. Click the Enter icon to proceed. Click the rule tile to view the rule in the output panel. Tip: The more context you give, the better the result. A detailed threat report that describes attacker techniques, tools, and command-line activity gives AI more behaviors to turn into rules. What to Do After the Rule Is Generated Generating the rule is the first step. Once your behavior rule or rules are ready, the next steps below help you get them into production and make sure your team understands them. Save and translate Once the rule is generated, you can take it into your workflow in a few clicks: Copy to clipboard: paste the rule straight into your system and start working with it right away. Save As > File.txt: download the rule as a file to share it, archive it, or use it outside the platform. Save As > New Rule: store the rule in a custom repository, so your team has one place for all the detection content it creates. Translate: convert the Sigma rule into the query language of your security stack, so the same detection works across different tools and isn’t tied to one platform. Understand the rule: summaries and decision tree Without leaving the generated rule, you can use three AI tools to help your team review, document, and triage faster: Short Summary: a concise, plain-language overview of what the rule detects. Use it for ticket descriptions, handover notes, and quick peer reviews, so nobody has to read the full logic just to understand the purpose of a rule. Full Summary: a detailed explanation of how the rule works, including what behavior it looks for and why. It helps new analysts get up to speed, gives you ready material for detection documentation, and supports audits and coverage reviews where you need to explain what each rule does. Decision Tree: a visual map of the rule’s logic that shows how the detection conditions connect and how an analyst can work through an alert step by step. It helps SOC teams triage faster, reduces guesswork on unfamiliar alerts, and makes it easier to see where a rule might need tuning. To use any of them, select Analyze , choose the tool, and click the Enter icon. Validate before you deploy Catch errors before they reach production. Go to Translation mode in Prime Architect, open the Improve tab, paste your rule, confirm the detected language, select Validate in the dropdown, and click Improve . Make custom modifications with AI Every environment is different. Use the chat interface to adjust the rule to your needs, such as adding exclusions, narrowing the scope, or changing the logic, simply by describing what you want. Put the rule into action A detection only protects you once it is running. After you generate and review the rule, deploy it to your SIEM and let it start watching for the threat in your environment. Start Turning Intelligence into Detections With Behavior Rule with AI in Prime Architect, a threat report is no longer something your team reads and files away. It becomes working detection content in minutes. Open Prime Architect, paste your next threat report, and let agentic AI tools do the heavy lifting, while your team keeps control of every rule that goes into production.

items.title: Sextortion “help” firm took $60 million from victims, FTC alleges
items.summary: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has filed a complaint accusing Digital Forensics Corporation of exploiting people already targeted by sextortionists . We have talked about sextortion and recovery scams in the past, but we never looked specifically at the combination. Apparently, there is a lot of money to be made for those ruthless enough to take money from victims already in a state of panic. The FTC has accused Digital Forensics Corporation, its owner Dmitry Belkin, and affiliated companies of misleading sextortion victims into paying at least $60 million for assistance that, in numerous instances, they did not provide. A federal court has temporarily halted the defendants’ activities while the case proceeds. Most of the time, sextortion emails are a bluff sent to a large number of targets to see if one takes the bait. But sextortion can also involve intimate images that someone really possesses. In those cases, a criminal threatens to share the material unless the victim pays, sends more images, or complies with other demands. In those cases, victims can feel desperate, especially when the demands keep coming, and may look for help to make it stop. According to the FTC, Digital Forensics targeted people searching for that help through advertisements on Google, YouTube, X, and other platforms. The company allegedly claimed it could track down criminals worldwide, identify perpetrators, and provide law enforcement with evidence needed to make arrests. Digital Forensics allegedly charged between $1,499 and $20,000 for a “Phase 1” package. That was supposed to include communicating with the sextortionist, tracking their location, producing an investigative report, and reporting the crime to law enforcement. According to the FTC, Digital Forensics Corporation changed the victims’ account settings to block the sextortionist, fabricated chat transcripts, and presented pre-saved coordinates, often in Nigeria or the Philippines, as the sextortionist’s location. After collecting the first payment, the company allegedly pressured customers to purchase “Phase 2” services, supposedly providing ongoing account monitoring and further assistance. The FTC says the company did not follow through on those promises either. Another huge red flag was that the company also allegedly discouraged victims from blocking their blackmailers, contrary to law enforcement and expert advice. The allegations against Digital Forensics Corporation have not yet been decided by the court. How to stay safe Be wary of anyone who promises to stop the threats or pressures you to pay immediately. Help should offer clear information and realistic options. It should not turn your fear into another payment deadline. If someone is threatening to share intimate images, you do not have to handle it alone. Preserve the threats and account details. Keep the messages, usernames, and payment demands. Block the offender but do not delete your account or the messages, since they may help real investigators. Stop communicating and block the blackmailer. Do not pay them or give them access to your devices or financial accounts. Report the account using the platform’s safety tools. Tell someone you trust about the sextortion. A friend, family member, counselor, or other trusted adult can provide support while you decide what to do next. Report the crime. Contact local police. In the US, you can also report sextortion to the FBI . If it involves a minor, report it through the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s CyberTipline . If you have already paid a service that you believe misled you, keep its ads, messages, contract, and receipts, and report your experience to the FTC through ReportFraud.ftc.gov . If you’re unsure whether something is a scam or not, ask Malwarebytes Scam Guard . It can help you assess it and provide advice on next steps. Something feel off? Check it before you click. items.title: CVE-2026-76519: Critical Cisco Secure Email Gateway Zero-Day Exploited for Root Access
items.summary: Cisco has patched CVE-2026-76519, a critical zero-day vulnerability affecting Cisco Secure Email Gateway (SEG) that is already being exploited in real-world attacks. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and enables an unauthenticated remote attacker to write arbitrary files and execute commands with root privileges on vulnerable appliances. The vulnerability resides in the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) functionality of Cisco Secure Email Gateway and stems from improper handling of email attachments when the File Reputation service is enabled. An attacker can exploit the issue simply by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment through an affected gateway, without needing credentials or user interaction. Cisco disclosed the vulnerability on October 14, 2026, after its Product Security Incident Response Team (PSIRT) became aware of active exploitation during October. The company has not disclosed who is behind the attacks, how many appliances have been compromised, or what attackers have done after obtaining access. The vulnerability is especially concerning because Secure Email Gateway appliances are positioned directly in enterprise email infrastructure. Successful compromise with root privileges can provide attackers with extensive control over the security appliance, access to credentials and cryptographic material, and potentially a pathway toward additional systems. CISA has added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, requiring applicable U.S. federal civilian agencies to remediate it by October 17, 2026. Organizations can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to strengthen their defenses against emerging vulnerabilities and accelerate threat hunting, investigation, and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Security professionals can also use Prime Architect to turn emerging threat intelligence into detection logic, convert indicators into hunting queries, refine existing rules, and adapt detections to their organization’s telemetry. Contact Sales CVE-2026-76519 analysis CVE-2026-76519 affects physical and virtual Cisco Secure Email Gateway appliances running vulnerable Cisco AsyncOS releases when two specific conditions are present: the File Reputation service is enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and the installed Content Scanner Tools version is earlier than 25.3.0.5525. Cisco classifies the vulnerability under CWE-23, Relative Path Traversal. Improper processing of email attachments in the Advanced Malware Protection feature allows a specially crafted attachment to manipulate file paths and cause arbitrary files to be written to the appliance’s underlying operating system. The attack requires no authentication. A threat actor only needs to send an email containing the malicious attachment through a vulnerable gateway. No recipient needs to open the message or interact with the attachment for the gateway itself to process the content. Successful exploitation can progress beyond arbitrary file creation. Cisco confirms that attackers can use the weakness to execute commands with root privileges on the operating system, effectively providing complete control over the compromised appliance. The vulnerability received a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 with the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. The combination of remote accessibility, low attack complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction explains its critical rating. Cisco Secure Email and Web Manager and Cisco Secure Web Appliance are not affected by this vulnerability. Cisco Secure Email Cloud environments have already received the corrected Content Scanner Tools package through Cisco’s managed upgrade process. The company discovered the flaw during internal security scanning. Although the dedicated advisory was released on October 14, Cisco had already shipped corrected AsyncOS releases 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780 as part of its September 14 security hardening release. The specific flaw received its own CVE and advisory after Cisco confirmed exploitation in the wild. This is not the first actively exploited Secure Email Gateway vulnerability disclosed recently. In September 2026, Cisco patched CVE-2026-76461, another flaw triggered through malicious email processing that could lead to unauthenticated command execution with root privileges. Cisco has not linked the two exploitation campaigns. At the time of writing, Cisco and the referenced reports have not documented a publicly validated CVE-2026-76519 PoC. However, active exploitation means defenders should consider vulnerable appliances at immediate risk regardless of whether public exploit code becomes available. For CVE-2026-76519 detection, Cisco provides a built-in security check that administrators can run against the appliance’s system_logs. Organizations should also examine external network and firewall telemetry because attackers with root privileges may be able to remove or conceal evidence directly on a compromised gateway. CVE-2026-76519 Mitigation Cisco has released fixes and states that no workaround fully addresses the vulnerability. Organizations operating affected Secure Email Gateway deployments should therefore apply the updated Content Scanner Tools package or migrate to a fixed AsyncOS release without delay. The first fixed releases include: AsyncOS 15.5: 15.5.5-014 AsyncOS 16.0: migrate to a fixed release AsyncOS 16.5: 16.5.0-780 Content Scanner Tools: 25.3.0.5525 or later Cisco recommends that organizations running AsyncOS releases earlier than 16.5 migrate to version 16.5.0-780. Importantly, the Content Scanner Tools update can also remediate supported installations without requiring an AsyncOS upgrade or appliance restart. Administrators can verify the currently installed scanner package by running contentscannerstatus from the CLI. Systems reporting Content Scanner Tools earlier than 25.3.0.5525 remain exposed when File Reputation is active. Customers who have enabled automatic Content Scanner Tools updates should verify that version 25.3.0.5525 or newer has actually been installed. Where automatic updates are disabled, administrators can trigger the update manually using the contentscannerupdate command. To Detect CVE-2026-76519 exploitation attempts, Cisco recommends reviewing system_logs for its System Security compromise scan. Administrators can use grep “System Security” system_logs and should perform this check individually on every Secure Email Gateway appliance that belongs to a cluster. A log entry stating System Security: Suspected compromise indicator was found indicates that compromise artifacts have been detected and organizations should follow Cisco’s incident-response guidance and contact Cisco TAC. A message stating that the security scan did not complete also requires escalation to TAC. These Cisco-provided messages represent the primary published CVE-2026-76519 IOCs available from the vendor. However, a clean local scan cannot definitively rule out compromise because successful attackers operate with root privileges and may remove or hide evidence. Cisco therefore recommends reviewing firewall and network telemetry stored outside the appliance for suspicious activity, including unexpected uploads initiated by the gateway, unusual downloads from external infrastructure, and anomalous connections involving potentially malicious IP addresses. Incident response differs depending on the appliance type. For potentially compromised physical appliances, Cisco recommends contacting TAC. For virtual appliances, defenders should preserve forensic evidence before making changes because upgrading an already compromised system can destroy relevant logs and artifacts. Cisco recommends rebuilding compromised virtual appliances using a fixed software release rather than simply upgrading them in place. Administrators should reconstruct the configuration without importing the previous configuration file and renew credentials and cryptographic materials stored on the appliance. Organizations using clustered Secure Email Gateway deployments require particular caution. Cluster members authenticate to one another using SSH key pairs, and root-level compromise can expose private keys used for this communication. An attacker who obtains those keys may potentially extend access to additional cluster members. FAQ What is CVE-2026-76519 and how does it work? CVE-2026-76519 is a critical relative path traversal vulnerability in the Advanced Malware Protection feature of Cisco Secure Email Gateway. An unauthenticated attacker can send a specially crafted email attachment through a vulnerable appliance, causing arbitrary files to be written to the operating system and potentially enabling command execution with root privileges. When was CVE-2026-76519 first discovered? Cisco discovered the vulnerability through internal security scanning, but the company has not disclosed the precise discovery date. Fixes were already included in security hardening releases published on September 14, 2026. Cisco issued a dedicated advisory on October 14 after PSIRT became aware of active exploitation. What is the impact of CVE-2026-76519 on systems? Successful exploitation can give an unauthenticated remote attacker root-level command execution on the Secure Email Gateway. This could allow modification of the appliance, credential or cryptographic-key theft, persistence, manipulation of email security functions, removal of forensic evidence, and potential follow-on compromise of connected or clustered systems. Can CVE-2026-76519 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Physical or virtual Cisco Secure Email Gateway appliances remain vulnerable when File Reputation is enabled and assigned to a mail policy and their Content Scanner Tools version is older than 25.3.0.5525. The risk is immediate because Cisco has confirmed active exploitation and CISA has added the vulnerability to its KEV catalog. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-76519? Upgrade to a fixed AsyncOS release or install Content Scanner Tools 25.3.0.5525 or later. Verify the update rather than assuming automatic deployment succeeded, run Cisco’s System Security compromise check, and investigate external network telemetry for suspicious activity. If compromise is suspected, preserve forensic evidence before remediation and follow Cisco’s latest details for CVE-2026-76519.

items.title: CVE-2026-0322: Actively Exploited PAN-OS RCE Flaw Enables Root Access
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-0322, a high-severity remote code execution vulnerability affecting the management interface of PAN-OS. The flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.6 and enables an authenticated attacker with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges on a vulnerable appliance/system. Palo Alto Networks disclosed the issue on October 14, 2026, confirming that very limited exploitation had already been observed against PAN-OS management interfaces. The vulnerability impacts PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls as well as Panorama virtual and M-Series appliances. Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected. The vulnerability is particularly significant because firewall management interfaces provide privileged control over devices positioned at critical network boundaries. Root-level compromise of such infrastructure can give attackers substantial control over firewall configuration and security operations and create opportunities for further activity against protected environments. CISA has also added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, requiring applicable U.S. federal civilian agencies to remediate it by October 17, 2026. Organizations can strengthen defenses against emerging vulnerability exploitation with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, which helps security teams operationalize threat intelligence, accelerate threat hunting, and apply relevant detection content across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Security professionals can also use Prime Architect to research emerging threats, generate and refine detection logic, convert indicators into hunting queries, and adapt detections to organizational telemetry. Contact Sales CVE-2026-0322 analysis CVE-2026-0322 affects the PAN-OS management interface and is classified as a code injection vulnerability under CWE-94, Improper Control of Generation of Code. An attacker who already possesses valid credentials and can reach the management interface can exploit the weakness to execute arbitrary code as root on the affected device. Unlike vulnerabilities that permit unauthenticated compromise directly from the internet, this flaw requires high privileges. However, that prerequisite does not eliminate the risk. Administrative credentials can be obtained through phishing, credential theft, reuse of compromised passwords, or earlier stages of an intrusion. Once those credentials are available, successful exploitation can transform management access into complete operating-system-level control of the firewall. Palo Alto Networks states that no special product configuration is required for a vulnerable version to be affected. Exposure is highest when the PAN-OS management interface can be reached from external IP addresses, particularly from the public internet. The vendor recommends limiting management access to trusted internal addresses and preferably allowing access only through a designated jump box. The affected product range includes PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2 across supported PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama appliances. The precise vulnerable build depends on the release branch. Palo Alto Networks confirms that Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are unaffected. The issue carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.6 with low attack complexity, no attack requirements, no user interaction, and high impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Its privilege requirement is rated high because exploitation requires an authenticated management user. Successful exploitation runs attacker-controlled code with root privileges. This level of access is particularly dangerous on a firewall or centralized Panorama management appliance because root privileges can potentially allow attackers to interfere with configurations, inspect local data, establish persistence, modify security controls, or use the compromised system as part of a broader intrusion. Palo Alto Networks discovered the vulnerability internally and credited senior principal product security researcher Suraj Siddharudh with identifying and reporting the flaw. The vendor published its security advisory on October 14, 2026. The company has confirmed “very limited exploitation” targeting PAN-OS management interfaces but has not disclosed the identity of the threat actors, the number or type of organizations targeted, or the specific post-exploitation activity observed. SecurityWeek similarly reports that no information has yet been released regarding the attackers behind the campaign. At the time of publication, the primary sources reviewed do not document a publicly available CVE-2026-0322 PoC. However, confirmed exploitation in real-world attacks means organizations should treat remediation as urgent regardless of whether public exploit code is available. Palo Alto Networks has shared three IP addresses associated with observed threat activity and limited exploit attempts: 66.42.72[.]14, 208.83.239[.]114, and 149.248.47[.]234. These indicators can support retrospective investigations, although security teams should not treat the absence of traffic from these addresses as proof that a system has not been targeted. For CVE-2026-0322 detection, defenders should review management-interface authentication and access telemetry for anomalous administrative activity, unexpected source addresses, unusual login patterns, and suspicious actions occurring shortly after successful authentication. Because successful exploitation results in root-level code execution, teams should also investigate abnormal system processes, unexpected configuration modifications, suspicious outbound network connections, newly created files, or other activity inconsistent with routine firewall administration. CVE-2026-0322 Mitigation Palo Alto Networks recommends upgrading affected PAN-OS installations to the appropriate fixed release as soon as possible. There is no known complete workaround for the vulnerability. The vendor lists the following patched release thresholds: PAN-OS 12.2: 12.2.4 or later; PAN-OS 12.1: applicable fixed builds include 12.1.4-h12, 12.1.7-h8, and 12.1.10-h2; PAN-OS 11.2: applicable fixes include 11.2.4-h22, 11.2.7-h21, 11.2.10-h15, 11.2.13-h3, and 11.2.16; PAN-OS 11.1: fixes include 11.1.4-h37, 11.1.6-h39, 11.1.7-h11, 11.1.10-h35, 11.1.13-h15, and 11.1.16-h3; PAN-OS 10.2: fixes include 10.2.7-h38, 10.2.10-h41, 10.2.13-h26, 10.2.16-h11, and 10.2.18-h12. Administrators running unsupported releases should migrate to a supported fixed version. As an immediate risk-reduction measure, organizations should ensure that PAN-OS management interfaces are not exposed broadly to the internet. Palo Alto Networks recommends restricting access to trusted internal IP addresses and, where possible, allowing management connectivity only from a dedicated jump box. Customers with a Threat Prevention subscription can obtain limited protection using Threat IDs 510046 and 510047 beginning with Applications and Threats content version 9159-10287. However, this protection has additional requirements, including routing management traffic through a data-plane interface, decrypting inbound management traffic, and enabling Threat Prevention inspection.
