Palo Alto Networks has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-0322, a high-severity remote code execution vulnerability affecting the management interface of PAN-OS. The flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.6 and enables an authenticated attacker with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges on a vulnerable appliance/system.

Palo Alto Networks disclosed the issue on October 14, 2026, confirming that very limited exploitation had already been observed against PAN-OS management interfaces. The vulnerability impacts PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls as well as Panorama virtual and M-Series appliances. Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected.

The vulnerability is particularly significant because firewall management interfaces provide privileged control over devices positioned at critical network boundaries. Root-level compromise of such infrastructure can give attackers substantial control over firewall configuration and security operations and create opportunities for further activity against protected environments.

CISA has also added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, requiring applicable U.S. federal civilian agencies to remediate it by October 17, 2026.

Organizations can strengthen defenses against emerging vulnerability exploitation with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, which helps security teams operationalize threat intelligence, accelerate threat hunting, and apply relevant detection content across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Security professionals can also use Prime Architect to research emerging threats, generate and refine detection logic, convert indicators into hunting queries, and adapt detections to organizational telemetry.

Contact Sales

CVE-2026-0322 analysis

CVE-2026-0322 affects the PAN-OS management interface and is classified as a code injection vulnerability under CWE-94, Improper Control of Generation of Code. An attacker who already possesses valid credentials and can reach the management interface can exploit the weakness to execute arbitrary code as root on the affected device.

Unlike vulnerabilities that permit unauthenticated compromise directly from the internet, this flaw requires high privileges. However, that prerequisite does not eliminate the risk. Administrative credentials can be obtained through phishing, credential theft, reuse of compromised passwords, or earlier stages of an intrusion. Once those credentials are available, successful exploitation can transform management access into complete operating-system-level control of the firewall.

Palo Alto Networks states that no special product configuration is required for a vulnerable version to be affected. Exposure is highest when the PAN-OS management interface can be reached from external IP addresses, particularly from the public internet. The vendor recommends limiting management access to trusted internal addresses and preferably allowing access only through a designated jump box.

The affected product range includes PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2 across supported PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama appliances. The precise vulnerable build depends on the release branch. Palo Alto Networks confirms that Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are unaffected.

The issue carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.6 with low attack complexity, no attack requirements, no user interaction, and high impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Its privilege requirement is rated high because exploitation requires an authenticated management user.

Successful exploitation runs attacker-controlled code with root privileges. This level of access is particularly dangerous on a firewall or centralized Panorama management appliance because root privileges can potentially allow attackers to interfere with configurations, inspect local data, establish persistence, modify security controls, or use the compromised system as part of a broader intrusion.

Palo Alto Networks discovered the vulnerability internally and credited senior principal product security researcher Suraj Siddharudh with identifying and reporting the flaw. The vendor published its security advisory on October 14, 2026.

The company has confirmed “very limited exploitation” targeting PAN-OS management interfaces but has not disclosed the identity of the threat actors, the number or type of organizations targeted, or the specific post-exploitation activity observed. SecurityWeek similarly reports that no information has yet been released regarding the attackers behind the campaign.

At the time of publication, the primary sources reviewed do not document a publicly available CVE-2026-0322 PoC. However, confirmed exploitation in real-world attacks means organizations should treat remediation as urgent regardless of whether public exploit code is available.

Palo Alto Networks has shared three IP addresses associated with observed threat activity and limited exploit attempts: 66.42.72[.]14, 208.83.239[.]114, and 149.248.47[.]234. These indicators can support retrospective investigations, although security teams should not treat the absence of traffic from these addresses as proof that a system has not been targeted.

For CVE-2026-0322 detection, defenders should review management-interface authentication and access telemetry for anomalous administrative activity, unexpected source addresses, unusual login patterns, and suspicious actions occurring shortly after successful authentication.

Because successful exploitation results in root-level code execution, teams should also investigate abnormal system processes, unexpected configuration modifications, suspicious outbound network connections, newly created files, or other activity inconsistent with routine firewall administration.

CVE-2026-0322 Mitigation

Palo Alto Networks recommends upgrading affected PAN-OS installations to the appropriate fixed release as soon as possible. There is no known complete workaround for the vulnerability.

The vendor lists the following patched release thresholds:

  • PAN-OS 12.2: 12.2.4 or later; PAN-OS 12.1: applicable fixed builds include 12.1.4-h12, 12.1.7-h8, and 12.1.10-h2; PAN-OS 11.2: applicable fixes include 11.2.4-h22, 11.2.7-h21, 11.2.10-h15, 11.2.13-h3, and 11.2.16; PAN-OS 11.1: fixes include 11.1.4-h37, 11.1.6-h39, 11.1.7-h11, 11.1.10-h35, 11.1.13-h15, and 11.1.16-h3; PAN-OS 10.2: fixes include 10.2.7-h38, 10.2.10-h41, 10.2.13-h26, 10.2.16-h11, and 10.2.18-h12. Administrators running unsupported releases should migrate to a supported fixed version.

As an immediate risk-reduction measure, organizations should ensure that PAN-OS management interfaces are not exposed broadly to the internet. Palo Alto Networks recommends restricting access to trusted internal IP addresses and, where possible, allowing management connectivity only from a dedicated jump box.

Customers with a Threat Prevention subscription can obtain limited protection using Threat IDs 510046 and 510047 beginning with Applications and Threats content version 9159-10287. However, this protection has additional requirements, including routing management traffic through a data-plane interface, decrypting inbound management traffic, and enabling Threat Prevention inspection. The vendor explicitly describes this as limited coverage rather than a substitute for upgrading.

To Detect CVE-2026-0322 exploitation, security teams should correlate successful management-interface authentication with unusual command execution, administrative changes, or system behavior. Particular attention should be given to management sessions originating from unexpected external addresses or accounts whose normal operational patterns do not include direct firewall administration.

The published CVE-2026-0322 IOCs include 66.42.72[.]14, 208.83.239[.]114, and 149.248.47[.]234. Organizations should search historical network and management logs for interactions involving these addresses while also hunting for broader behavioral evidence of compromise.

If suspicious exploitation is identified, affected appliances should be investigated for unauthorized configuration changes and abnormal processes or connections. Administrative credentials associated with the device should be considered potentially exposed and rotated after containment where appropriate.

items.title: Raven AI lets cops find your home from a photo taken inside
items.summary: Photos you take with your phone and some digital cameras can contain hidden information, including where they were taken. You can strip that data out before sharing a photo with someone, which would help to protect your location. But the image itself may still give you away. A company called Graylark says its Raven AI tool can match an indoor photo to a specific property using visual clues alone. No GPS data or view out of the window required. We’ve seen this company before . Its tool, GeoSpy, could work out where a photo was taken by analyzing features in the image, such as vegetation, buildings, and other landmarks. Graylark itself grew out of experiments founder Daniel Heinen and his brothers carried out after reading about using AI to play GeoGuessr , a geography game in which people look at street-level images and try to work out where they were taken. The company has since taken it further. According to 404 Media , Graylark has renamed the tool as Raven and expanded it to identify indoor locations as well. It uses visual clues in the image, without needing location metadata. The tool works by matching images against property photos. An image of something as banal as a washer/dryer sitting in a nook can return a list of ranked results. The tool’s Short-Term Rental ID feature can search what Graylark describes as millions of rental listings worldwide, using an interior photo or a frame from a video. However, the system targets more than just rental properties. Its Find Property feature searches for properties using exterior photos and, now, interior ones in supported cities. This is more than just reverse image search, which can help you see if the same photo you’re looking at has been used elsewhere. The service can match different views of the same property by identifying features ranging from the shapes of wall tiles to the structure of a room and the color of its surfaces. Law enforcement is already using the tool, for which founder Daniel Heinen landed $10.7m in seed funding in August. 404 Media said that Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office and the Los Angeles Police Department bought access to the product. According to Heinen’s social media posts, Raven can now tell which hotel you stayed in from a single photo. He cited a feature called HotelID that isn’t yet listed on the website. The Raven website also cites other uses. For example, it can tell you a car’s exact make, model, and year from a picture of its interior. The tool works from identifiers such as email addresses, too. Investigators can find public photos on linked accounts and then use those photos to look for location clues. Graylark says this does not give investigators access to private accounts or messages. Heinen says the short-term rental feature uses images from millions of rental listings around the world. According to 404 Media, Airbnb said it had no relationship with Graylark, and Zillow said scraping was against its terms of service. Those statements don’t confirm how Graylark obtained its imagery. Heinen’s ambitions don’t seem to stop here. On September 8, he mentioned that he was experimenting with recent footage from tens of thousands of dashcams. He has said that this kind of system can help combat human trafficking. A George Mason University study found that in around 80% of federal sex trafficking cases active in 2018 and 2019, victims were exploited at hotels or motels. And perhaps AI can help with unsolved crimes if used properly . Any suggested location still needs to be checked against other evidence. But technology can also be misused, particularly when it comes to stalking. Heinen said on X that Raven is only available to enterprises, government, and law enforcement agencies. Other websites and consumer apps use the GeoSpy name, but Graylark says third-party products using that name are not operated by or affiliated with the company. This brings us to what you can do to protect yourself should someone use this kind of tool for nefarious purposes. How to keep your home more private Think before publishing interior or exterior pictures of your home online. Even Google Photos can estimate where a photo was taken using landmarks and similarities with your other photos that have known locations, it says . Check the frame for distinctive features before posting. Look for distinctive tiles, room layouts, views through windows, house numbers, or mail showing your address. Crop these out where practical. Limit who can see your photos. Review the audience for your social posts and photo albums, including older ones. When traveling, consider waiting until you’ve left before posting recognizable accommodation photos. Review old property listings. Ask your agent and the relevant property websites whether they can remove interior photos from old listings. Removal cannot recall copies already downloaded or collected. If you’re advertising a rental, use approximate-location settings where available, but remember that the listing photos themselves may still identify the property. Remove location metadata before sharing. This won’t prevent visual matching, but it removes another way to find where a photo was taken. Don’t assume every service removes it for you. Apple users can do this directly on iOS : When sharing from Photos, tap Options and turn off Location . Google Photos lets you remove estimated or manually added locations, but not those recorded by your camera. Check location-sharing settings for each album, link, or conversation. Photos downloaded and shared outside Google Photos may still contain the original location data. Samsung users can choose to remove location data when sharing from Samsung Gallery , where the option is available. Browse like no one’s watching. items.title: Pluralistic: Expedia amazoned hotel rooms (15 Oct 2026)
items.summary: Today's links Expedia amazoned hotel rooms : Everything more expensive for everyone, monopolies everywhere, and we're all screwed. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : Delta v dovening; "Play Money"; Alabama's ethnic cleansing; We trust neuroscience over psychology; Billionaires' anti-homeless pogrom; Game devs v DRM; What security means; Microsoft, tear down that wall! Publisher won't revert rights; SNL's Trump/Clinton debate; Chicago Tribune's murder; AI after AI. Upcoming appearances : Paris, Vancouver, Victoria, Ottawa, Vienna, Kilkenny, Oxford, Sheffield, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. Expedia amazoned hotel rooms ( permalink ) No matter where you shop, you're getting screwed by Amazon. Amazon has found a way to make everything you buy – at Target, at a mom-and-pop shop, even direct from the manufacturer – more expensive. And they're not the only one: Expedia's done the same thing, but for hotel rooms. Here's how Amazon broke the economy: first, they locked in a key group of shoppers. The vast majority of affluent shoppers in the USA have Amazon Prime accounts. Having prepaid for a year's shipping in advance, those Prime subscribers start their purchasing journey by searching Amazon, and if they find what they're looking for, that's where it ends. America's affluent top decile – the 10% of richest Americans – do the majority of America's shopping, a phenomenon that has only been accelerated by America's precipitous slide into oligarchy, which has exhausted the savings and the credit-card limits and the home equity of the majority of Americans, who increasingly can't afford to buy anything: https://dreamagainusa.org/ If you want to sell things in America, you must sell them in the place where the top decile shops, and that's Amazon. For merchants, that is an incredibly expensive proposition: 51-60% of every dollar you spend with an independent merchant on Amazon is claimed by Amazon through junk fees, listing fees, commissions, processing fees and other scams: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/04/cheating-at-fraud/#absentee-rentier Merchants don't have 51-60% margins they can afford to turn over to Amazon. To remain viable while selling on Amazon, they have to raise prices. Amazon doesn't mind if prices go up, so long as Amazon's price remains competitive. So Amazon imposes a requirement on its suppliers called "most favored nation," which requires sellers to offer their best price on Amazon: https://pluralistic.net/2026/02/25/most-favored-nation/#price-fixing Practically speaking, that means that when you raise your price on Amazon, you must raise your prices everywhere by the same amount, which means that no matter where you shop (Target, Walmart, the corner store or direct from the factory), you pay the Amazon Tax. The Amazon Tax is a prime (you should forgive the expression) example of enshittification, in which an intermediary (a business that sits between buyers and sellers, AKA, "a platform") screws both customers and sellers to benefit itself. But Amazon isn't the only example of a powerful digital intermediary that has used its market power to impose an economy-wide tax. Wherever you look online, you find digital giants who grew the way Amazon grew (buying all of their competitors) and then did what Amazon did (squeezing buyers and sellers, making prices higher everywhere). That's what happened with Expedia. Almost every travel site you can find online has been purchased by Expedia (Hotels.com, Travelocity, and Orbitz), and the ones that aren't Expedia subsidiaries were acquired by its main rival, Priceline (Booking.com, Kayak, Agoda and even Opentable). Nearly all the hotel rooms are booked by a tiny minority of travelers – largely that same top decile that Amazon has so thoroughly captured and locked in – and hoteliers can't live without their business, and they're almost all Expedia and/or Priceline customers. Expedia accounts for 80% of all hotel bookings by dollar value. Expedia's position, in other words, is basically Amazon's position, so Expedia is doing exactly what Amazon is doing: they charge huge fees to hotels, and then force the hotels to raise their prices everywhere through a "most favored nation" deal: https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.wawd.369601/gov.uscourts.wawd.369601.1.0.pdf But – as Lee Hepner writes for the BIG newsletter – Expedia has figured out ways to out-Amazon Amazon. They've copied one of Amazon's sleaziest businesses, and made it worse : https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/how-expedia-rigs-travel-markets-and Here's Amazon's sleaziest commercial practice: when you search Amazon, the top results for your search aren't the best matches for your queries; they're products sold by the companies willing to pay the most for search placement, in a "real-time auction" that runs every time you search. The cost of winning that auction comes out of your pocket through higher prices: the first result for an Amazon query is, on average, 29% more expensive than the best match. The top row is 25% more expensive. On average, the best match for your query is 17 positions down the screen, on the second page, where almost no one ever bothers to scroll: https://pluralistic.net/2023/11/03/subprime-attention-rent-crisis/#euthanize-rentiers This rip-off is Amazon's most profitable line of business, more profitable than AWS or Prime. It makes the company more than $80b/year . And – incredibly – Expedia's found a way to make it even worse. Like Amazon, Expedia auctions off its search results. They call this their "VIP listing" program. Practically speaking, hotels have to pay for this, because it boosts booking rates by 42% (the first ten results on an Expedia search-results page get 62% of the clicks). VIP listing is expensive for the merchant – but it's even more expensive for you and me. That's because Expedia requires hotels in its VIP listings programs to raise their prices on non-Expedia sites by 10-25%…INDEFINITELY. Let me repeat that: to stay in business, hotels need to be on Expedia. To stay in business on Expedia, hotels have to raise their prices to pay Expedia's junk fees, but they have to raise their prices everywhere else. But to really stay in business on Expedia, hotels have to use the VIP program, which is even more expensive. And – one more time – hotels in the VIP program have to jack up their prices everywhere else, INDEFINITELY . This means that, throughout the economy, hotel prices are rising at a superinflationary rate, because Expedia – who command 80% of the market – are pushing those prices up. This goes a long way to explaining why US hotel rates rose 58% from a 2020 average of $103/night to a 2025 average of $162/night. It explains why hotel prices rose by 5% last year , which is double the rate of inflation. And this is why Expedia stock is up 65% since the start of the Iran war, a fact that Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin attributes to "higher margins" from "higher prices": https://s202.q4cdn.com/757635260/files/doc_financials/2026/q2/Q2-2026-Earnings-Presentation-Final.pdf In his coverage of the Expedia lawsuit – which brought many of these details to light – Hepner notes that hotels themselves have undergone near-total cartelization, with Hilton, Marriott, and Choice International owning the majority of all hotels after a string of acquisitions that went largely unchallenged by slumbering antitrust regulators around the world. These consolidated chains have also jacked up prices and enshittified their service, slashing housekeeping and check-in staff and allowing their facilities to slip into disrepair. This, too, is characteristic of monopolization: whenever a monopoly takes over part of its supply chain, the rest of the supply chain consolidates to prevent itself from being ripped off by the new giant. This is the story of publishers consolidating to defend themselves from Borders/B&N, Walmart and Costco, then Amazon; and it's the story of literary agencies consolidating to resist the power of those overgrown publishers. And it's the story of health-care, which saw consolidation in pharmaceuticals leading to mergers among hospitals, who screwed the insurers, who also consolidated. In every case, it's the workers and the people who rely on them that get the shitty end of the stick. Hotel guests, readers and patients pay more for inferior products. Writers, editors, doctors, nurses, hotel staff and housekeepers get lower pay and worse working-conditions: https://pluralistic.net/2024/12/18/loose-flapping-ends/#luigi-has-a-point There is nothing wrong with the idea of an intermediary. Most writers can't publish and sell their own books, and few travelers can navigate finding hotels in strange cities without help. The problem of intermediaries is that when intermediaries gain monopoly power – by buying their rivals and capturing buyers and sellers – they are able to squeeze both. As Tim Wu says, this is the moment when a company that's supposed to be helping becomes a predator, acquires "main character syndrome" and makes every transaction all about the middleman, at the expense of the people buying and selling: https://pluralistic.net/2026/08/05/absentee-landlord/ There are so many reasons for inflation and the cost of living crisis: wage stagnation, wars of choice in Iran, environmental cataclysm after environmental cataclysm. But under cover of these real factors is a cohort of what Matt Stoller calls "economic termites," parasites that have infested the walls of our economy and are devouring it from within. You can't solve this by shopping. Calling the hotel direct won't fix it: they have to be on Expedia to survive, and to be on Expedia, they have to sign up for VIP service, and to keep VIP service, they have to make their prices higher everywhere. To fix this, we need systemic action: the corporate death penalty for the companies that are consuming the structural members of our society. Expedia amazoned hotel rooms (permalink)

No matter where you shop, you're getting screwed by Amazon. Amazon has found a way to make everything you buy – at Target, at a mom-and-pop shop, even direct from the manufacturer – more expensive. And they're not the only one: Expedia's done the same thing, but for hotel rooms.

Here's how Amazon broke the economy: first, they locked in a key group of shoppers. The vast majority of affluent shoppers in the USA have Amazon Prime accounts. Having prepaid for a year's shipping in advance, those Prime subscribers start their purchasing journey by searching Amazon, and if they find what they're looking for, that's where it ends.

America's affluent top decile – the 10% of richest Americans – do the majority of America's shopping, a phenomenon that has only been accelerated by America's precipitous slide into oligarchy, which has exhausted the savings and the credit-card limits and the home equity of the majority of Americans, who increasingly can't afford to buy anything:

https://dreamagainusa.org/

If you want to sell things in America, you must sell them in the place where the top decile shops, and that's Amazon. For merchants, that is an incredibly expensive proposition: 51-60% of every dollar you spend with an independent merchant on Amazon is claimed by Amazon through junk fees, listing fees, commissions, processing fees and other scams:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/04/cheating-at-fraud/#absentee-rentier

Merchants don't have 51-60% margins they can afford to turn over to Amazon. To remain viable while selling on Amazon, they have to raise prices. Amazon doesn't mind if prices go up, so long as Amazon's price remains competitive. So Amazon imposes a requirement on its suppliers called "most favored nation," which requires sellers to offer their best price on Amazon:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/02/25/most-favored-nation/#price-fixing

Practically speaking, that means that when you raise your price on Amazon, you must raise your prices everywhere by the same amount, which means that no matter where you shop (Target, Walmart, the corner store or direct from the factory), you pay the Amazon Tax.

The Amazon Tax is a prime (you should forgive the expression) example of enshittification, in which an intermediary (a business that sits between buyers and sellers, AKA, "a platform") screws both customers and sellers to benefit itself.

But Amazon isn't the only example of a powerful digital intermediary that has used its market power to impose an economy-wide tax. Wherever you look online, you find digital giants who grew the way Amazon grew (buying all of their competitors) and then did what Amazon did (squeezing buyers and sellers, making prices higher everywhere).

That's what happened with Expedia. Almost every travel site you can find online has been purchased by Expedia (Hotels.com, Travelocity, and Orbitz), and the ones that aren't Expedia subsidiaries were acquired by its main rival, Priceline (Booking.com, Kayak, Agoda and even Opentable). Nearly all the hotel rooms are booked by a tiny minority of travelers – largely that same top decile that Amazon has so thoroughly captured and locked in – and hoteliers can't live without their business, and they're almost all Expedia and/or Priceline customers. Expedia accounts for 80% of all hotel bookings by dollar value.

Expedia's position, in other words, is basically Amazon's position, so Expedia is doing exactly what Amazon is doing: they charge huge fees to hotels, and then force the hotels to raise their prices everywhere through a "most favored nation" deal:

https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.wawd.369601/gov.uscourts.wawd.369601.1.0.pdf

But – as Lee Hepner writes for the BIG newsletter – Expedia has figured out ways to out-Amazon Amazon. They've copied one of Amazon's sleaziest businesses, and made it worse:

https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/how-expedia-rigs-travel-markets-and

Here's Amazon's sleaziest commercial practice: when you search Amazon, the top results for your search aren't the best matches for your queries; they're products sold by the companies willing to pay the most for search placement, in a "real-time auction" that runs every time you search. The cost of winning that auction comes out of your pocket through higher prices: the first result for an Amazon query is, on average, 29% more expensive than the best match. The top row is 25% more expensive. On average, the best match for your query is 17 positions down the screen, on the second page, where almost no one ever bothers to scroll:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/11/03/subprime-attention-rent-crisis/#euthanize-rentiers

This rip-off is Amazon's most profitable line of business, more profitable than AWS or Prime. It makes the company more than $80b/year. And – incredibly – Expedia's found a way to make it even worse.

Like Amazon, Expedia auctions off its search results. They call this their "VIP listing" program. Practically speaking, hotels have to pay for this, because it boosts booking rates by 42% (the first ten results on an Expedia search-results page get 62% of the clicks). VIP listing is expensive for the merchant – but it's even more expensive for you and me.

That's because Expedia requires hotels in its VIP listings programs to raise their prices on non-Expedia sites by 10-25%…INDEFINITELY.

Let me repeat that: to stay in business, hotels need to be on Expedia. To stay in business on Expedia, hotels have to raise their prices to pay Expedia's junk fees, but they have to raise their prices everywhere else. But to really stay in business on Expedia, hotels have to use the VIP program, which is even more expensive. And – one more time – hotels in the VIP program have to jack up their prices everywhere else, INDEFINITELY. This means that, throughout the economy, hotel prices are rising at a superinflationary rate, because Expedia – who command 80% of the market – are pushing those prices up.

This goes a long way to explaining why US hotel rates rose 58% from a 2020 average of $103/night to a 2025 average of $162/night. It explains why hotel prices rose by 5% last year, which is double the rate of inflation. And this is why Expedia stock is up 65% since the start of the Iran war, a fact that Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin attributes to "higher margins" from "higher prices":

https://s202.q4cdn.com/757635260/files/doc_financials/2026/q2/Q2-2026-Earnings-Presentation-Final.pdf

In his coverage of the Expedia lawsuit – which brought many of these details to light – Hepner notes that hotels themselves have undergone near-total cartelization, with Hilton, Marriott, and Choice International owning the majority of all hotels after a string of acquisitions that went largely unchallenged by slumbering antitrust regulators around the world. These consolidated chains have also jacked up prices and enshittified their service, slashing housekeeping and check-in staff and allowing their facilities to slip into disrepair.

This, too, is characteristic of monopolization: whenever a monopoly takes over part of its supply chain, the rest of the supply chain consolidates to prevent itself from being ripped off by the new giant. This is the story of publishers consolidating to defend themselves from Borders/B&N, Walmart and Costco, then Amazon; and it's the story of literary agencies consolidating to resist the power of those overgrown publishers.

And it's the story of health-care, which saw consolidation in pharmaceuticals leading to mergers among hospitals, who screwed the insurers, who also consolidated.

In every case, it's the workers and the people who rely on them that get the shitty end of the stick. Hotel guests, readers and patients pay more for inferior products. Writers, editors, doctors, nurses, hotel staff and housekeepers get lower pay and worse working-conditions:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/12/18/loose-flapping-ends/#luigi-has-a-point

There is nothing wrong with the idea of an intermediary. Most writers can't publish and sell their own books, and few travelers can navigate finding hotels in strange cities without help. The problem of intermediaries is that when intermediaries gain monopoly power – by buying their rivals and capturing buyers and sellers – they are able to squeeze both. As Tim Wu says, this is the moment when a company that's supposed to be helping becomes a predator, acquires "main character syndrome" and makes every transaction all about the middleman, at the expense of the people buying and selling:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/08/05/absentee-landlord/

There are so many reasons for inflation and the cost of living crisis: wage stagnation, wars of choice in Iran, environmental cataclysm after environmental cataclysm. But under cover of these real factors is a cohort of what Matt Stoller calls "economic termites," parasites that have infested the walls of our economy and are devouring it from within.

You can't solve this by shopping. Calling the hotel direct won't fix it: they have to be on Expedia to survive, and to be on Expedia, they have to sign up for VIP service, and to keep VIP service, they have to make their prices higher everywhere. To fix this, we need systemic action: the corporate death penalty for the companies that are consuming the structural members of our society.

items.summary_html:
Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published.

Satellite imagery obtained by Bellingcat lays bare the extent of tree-felling at a Washington DC golf course that President Trump is reportedly seeking to transform into a championship-level course, despite moves to protect the site by conservationists. 

The extent and circumstances surrounding the rapid changes prompted a judge to call an emergency hearing earlier this week, banning any further changes until later this month.

Reports on Wednesday detailed that 430 trees were cut down at the East Potomac Golf Links  which is owned by the Federal government and managed by the National Park Service (NPS). This is despite a judge’s order issued earlier this year that required court approval to cut down more than 10 trees at the course. 

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes was reported to have said that the government’s actions had cost it “all of its credibility with me in this case.” 

She is also reported to have said she was “furious” with the Justice Department for the lack of time afforded the court and plaintiffs before the tree removal was carried out.

NPR reported that officials notified the court just before 5pm on Friday Oct. 9 of plans to remove up to 529 trees in phases starting  the very next day on Saturday Oct. 10. That prompted Reyes to call an emergency meeting on Oct. 12. By that time, 430 trees had reportedly been cut down.

Images taken at the course earlier this week show trunks and branches strewn out across fairways.

Just total devastation wrought on East Potomac Park this past weekend. 450+ trees. For an admin that professes to support “beautification” of DC, that’s sure not what we or anybody else who has seen what they did on Saturday would describe it as. East Potomac is (was?) a thriving, beautiful gem in the heart of Washington DC. A beautiful, public, accessible place that hundreds of thousands use annually. The assault on this place should infuriate every American. The impacts of what took place Saturday will take years to fix. We cannot sit idly by while this admin treats our public lands like they are for the taking.

— Save East Po (@SaveEastPo) October 13, 2026

But satellite imagery affords a broader look at exactly what sections of the course have been impacted.

The Image below from Planet Labs taken on October 8 shows the golf course before the tree-felling was carried out.

A satellite image from Planet Labs PBC shows the East Potomac Golf Links on October 8. Larger version visible here.

Planet Labs imagery captured on Oct. 13 shows large barren sections towards the south and west of the course, where trees were removed.

A satellite image from Planet Labs PBC shows the East Potomac Golf Links on October 13. Larger version visible here.

A before and after slider allows for easy comparison of the Oct. 8 and Oct.13 images.

Support Bellingcat

Your donations directly contribute to our ability to publish groundbreaking investigations and uncover wrongdoing around the world.

Donate

Reuters reported that an organisation called The ​DC Preservation League said in a February ​2026 lawsuit that President Donald Trump was flouting ⁠environmental laws to “irreparably destroy a priceless piece of American history” so he could “convert a public recreation space into an exclusive, high-end golf course.”

Kevin Griess, an NPS official, reportedly stated at Monday’s hearing that tree removal was part of a 2019 plan that predates Trump’s aims for the course and sought to restore links-style vegetation.

Bellingcat contacted NPS as well as the Department of Justice but did not receive a response before publication.

A golfer hits toward felled trees at the East Potomac Golf Links. REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

The changes to the golf course are not the only ones President Trump has sought in Washington DC and the surrounding area since the beginning of his second term. In October last year  demolition began on the East Wing of the White House with the aim of building a new ballroom claiming it was “the safest building ever built.”  

Trump has also proposed a 250-foot-tall “Triumphal Arch” to be built just outside the Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.

items.title: UAT-6275 Hackers Exploit WinRAR Flaw to Target CIS Government Organizations
items.summary: UAT-6275 hackers have used a known WinRAR flaw to plant malware on Windows systems while targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The activity shows how an unpatched archive tool can turn a routine attachment into lasting remote access, with the malicious program starting when the victim next signs in. The campaign involves CVE-2025-8088, a path traversal flaw that lets crafted archives write files outside the folder chosen for extraction. Researchers observed the group adding this method in April 2026, alongside older attacks using Word macros, executable downloaders, and malicious shortcuts. The wider activity reviewed ran from June 2025 through August 2026. Cisco Talos researchers, working with Recorded Future’s Insikt Group, identified the malware and linked the activity to UAT-6275, tracked by Recorded Future as TAG-193. Their October 14 research report describes custom reverse shells named PickleShell, Chvost, and Laplas. These tools let attackers send commands to infected computers and receive the results through remote connections. UAT-6275 Hackers Exploit WinRAR Flaw The WinRAR attack, classified as Chain D, used a RAR archive containing two visible PDF decoys. Hidden inside were payload records that abused NTFS alternate data streams, a Windows file feature. The WinRAR path traversal flaw allowed those records to place PickleShell in the current user’s Startup folder instead of the expected extraction location. Lure document masquerading as a Russian diplomatic congratulatory letter (Source – Cisco Talos) The archive included ten hidden stream names pointing to the same payload, with different numbers of parent-folder steps. This approach helped account for different extraction locations. A successful write placed the executable in Startup without requiring administrator rights. The malware then ran at the next sign-in, giving the attacker a foothold without another prompt. PickleShell is a C#/.NET reverse shell that poses as a Windows service component. The analyzed payload starts a hidden command shell and passes command input and output to its control server. Later builds used encrypted connections. Researchers also found a stable identifier across nine samples, offering defenders another way to hunt for related files despite name changes. Earlier activity began with macro-enabled Word documents in June 2025. When a victim enabled macros, the document downloaded and ran another program. From July, PS2EXE downloaders packaged PowerShell scripts as Windows executables, fetched reverse-shell payloads, and created scheduled tasks to keep running. These stages show that the WinRAR exploit expanded an existing toolkit rather than replacing it. Four Delivery Paths Support Access From October 2025, malicious shortcuts launched PowerShell to retrieve scripts from GitHub. Later versions also downloaded PickleShell into Startup. Earlier Silent Lynx phishing campaigns used similar government-themed attachments and shortcuts. Talos reported overlap with Silent Lynx but continues to track UAT-6275 separately from YoroTrooper because direct indicator or toolset overlap between those two groups was not observed. Three exposed staging directories and a previously unreported GitHub repository gave investigators access to payloads, tool lists, and infrastructure changes. The repository’s history helped trace malware updates and control-server changes. Similar GitHub malware delivery methods appear in unrelated campaigns, underlining why defenders should examine script behavior rather than assume that downloads from a trusted platform are safe. Chain C retrieves a GitHub-hosted PowerShell script (Source – Cisco Talos) Observed victims and lure themes covered Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Belarus. The targeted work included diplomacy, economic planning, agriculture, environmental management, and energy. Decoys included an Armenian diplomatic letter and a proposal involving Turkmenistan’s Turkmennebit and Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery, suggesting interest in regional talks and resource supplies. Talos assessed a Kazakhstan connection with medium confidence, citing language clues, testing submissions, infrastructure access, and working hours consistent with UTC+5. That assessment does not establish government sponsorship. Investigators also recovered Linux-compatible tools and a public FortiWeb exploit, but the joint paper did not confirm that this actor had exploited FortiWeb systems in the wild. Organizations should update affected WinRAR installations to a supported release containing the fix introduced in version 7.13. Other WinRAR exploitation campaigns show why archive software deserves regular patch checks. Security teams should review unexpected Startup-folder files, new scheduled tasks, hidden PowerShell sessions, and scripts downloaded from public repositories, especially when these events follow archive extraction or suspicious email attachments. The finding also calls for careful incident review: removing the original RAR attachment does not remove a payload already written to Startup. Defenders should connect file creation, process execution, and outbound traffic when checking suspected infections. Talos published ClamAV signatures and Snort rules for coverage, while the joint technical paper provides hashes and network indicators that can support searches across endpoint records and retained logs during incident response and threat hunting. SHA-256 392b70086f10c23ce7b4173d1f68d72727ea0146260fb773c78642f6eb641775 PickleShell payload delivered through the WinRAR attack. SHA-256 cedc4ec0c238b1fc7a71dfa54f7d2d407539d22b87fe1c73b96b7a0dc17d4e40 Macro-enabled Word document representing Chain A. SHA-256 d12eef4b4b57c0186a166afc6246bf7fb4f668d0a84348c076c4943af1c98838 China–Central Asia Summit campaign sample. items.title: The GhostX Ecosystem: Forged in Transit, Licensed to Deceive
items.summary: Executive Summary Cyble has continued tracking GhostBat RAT activity targeting Android users in India since its initial identification in October 2025 . Recent investigations into malicious mParivahan and eChallan-themed applications revealed a broader operator-controlled ecosystem that we track as GhostX. Analysis of the exposed GhostX backend identified administrative and user-management structures, device-control records, SMS-delivery instructions, call-forwarding activity, and continuously changing phishing content , indicating active campaign management. Impressions The latest GhostBat RAT variant represents a significant evolution in both delivery and post-compromise capabilities. The malware now abuses the Android Accessibility Service to support Ghost Overlay and broader PIN/key-input capture targeting financial applications used across India. Ghost Overlay transparently intercepts PIN keypad interactions in Google Pay and MobiKwik. It replays the same touches into the legitimate application, allowing the malware to capture PIN information without presenting a conventional phishing interface. The variant also targets 60 banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and payment applications for broader PIN capture. Modus Operandi GhostBat RAT has diversified its loader architecture, with at least six observed delivery mechanisms, while the latest build uses libnetbridge.so and multiple cryptographic and custom container stages. Firebase Remote Config further enables operators to dynamically modify C&C infrastructure and malware functionality after installation. Figure 1 – GhostBat RAT Infection Chain Key Takeaways GhostBat RAT continues to target Android users in India via mParivahan- and eChallan-themed smishing campaigns, using phishing pages and public hosting platforms to distribute malicious APKs. Our investigation uncovered GhostX, a broader operator-controlled ecosystem that supports phishing, device management, backend configuration, and the distribution of the GhostBat RAT. The latest GhostBat RAT variant abuses the Android Accessibility Service, including the Ghost Overlay technique to intercept PIN entry in legitimate Google Pay and MobiKwik applications. The malware also implements broader PIN/key-input capture targeting 60 Android applications associated with India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital-payment ecosystem. GhostBat RAT’s delivery layer has evolved through multiple loader and dropper implementations, with the latest libnetbridge.so loader employing several transformations, including encryption, compression, and custom container stages, before recovering the final payload. Firebase Remote Config enables dynamic C&C and feature management, allowing operators to modify backend infrastructure and selected malware capabilities without rebuilding or redistributing the APK. Overview In October 2025, Cyble identified GhostBat RAT being distributed through MiningDropper and targeting Android users in India. We have since continued to track related activity and investigate malicious applications impersonating India’s mParivahan and eChallan services. This research uncovered a broader Android threat ecosystem that we track as GhostX, along with significantly evolved variants of GhostBat RAT. The most recent GhostBat RAT variant demonstrates a notable increase in capability and operational flexibility. It uses Firebase Remote Config to dynamically manage command-and-control (C&C) infrastructure and to enable or disable individual malware modules without requiring APK redistribution. This variant also implements a sophisticated Ghost Overlay technique targeting legitimate Google Pay and MobiKwik PIN-entry interfaces. Instead of displaying a conventional fake login page, the malware places transparent accessibility overlays over the legitimate application’s keypad, records the victim’s touch selections, and replays the same interaction into the genuine application. Additionally, the malware implements a PIN-capture capability through keylogging, targeting 60 Android applications across India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital payment ecosystem. The malware’s delivery and packing mechanisms have evolved considerably across the samples analyzed. We identified at least six distinct loader or dropper implementations, including: Native AES-CBC-protected APK containers Custom SPKZ/SPK1 payload formats Java-based in-memory DEX loaders Remote APK downloaders Multi-stage XOR/AES loaders A newer native libnetbridge.so loader using multiple cryptographic, transformation, compression, and custom container stages before recovering the final payload This diversification suggests continued investment in defeating static detection and complicating automated malware extraction. GhostBat RAT is primarily distributed via smishing messages that contain malicious links. When victims follow these links, they are redirected to phishing pages that impersonate either the legitimate Parivahan service or a Google Play-style application download page and are encouraged to install a fraudulent mParivahan APK (see Figures 2 and 3). During our investigation, we also repeatedly observed GitHub repositories and GitHub-hosted assets being used to distribute malicious APKs, providing attackers with readily available public hosting infrastructure. Figure 2 – Fake Google Play Store-style mParivahan installation website Figure 3 – Fake mParivahan website prompting to download APK file Discovery of the GhostX Ecosystem The GhostX investigation began with the discovery of multiple Android applications impersonating India’s mParivahan and eChallan ecosystem. Samples were collected from phishing infrastructure and public GitHub repositories containing APKs named or presented as mParivahan, vehicle-challan, traffic-enforcement, or other related government applications. Initial static analysis revealed that many of these APKs were only first-stage loaders. Their visible DEX code offered limited functionality, while the actual malware payload was either concealed within encrypted assets or retrieved later. After unpacking the applications to their final payloads, we identified multiple custom C&C infrastructures, Firebase projects, and overlapping Android surveillance and financial-fraud capabilities. A major breakthrough came from the analysis of a NextGen mParivahan sample whose unpacked payload contained the Firebase project identifier: ghostx-panel The exposed Firebase backend provided significantly greater visibility into the operator’s infrastructure and control workflow. The database contained structures including: clients bot_users admins admin_logins settings All_Users Verify_Device Analysis of the exposed GhostX backend revealed evidence of a structured operator-management layer beyond conventional malware C&C functionality. The database contained administrator and user records with role and account-status fields, a global session identifier, bot-user mappings, and dedicated admin_logins records containing device fingerprints, timestamps, and online status (see Figure 4). These artifacts indicate that GhostX incorporates an authentication and session management framework for operator-side access and management of compromised devices. The presence of distinct user, administrator, and bot-user roles suggests a multi-operator, service-oriented architecture. It raises the possibility that GhostX could support a Malware-as-a-Service-style operating model. Figure 4 – Exposed administrative records. During continued monitoring of the exposed infrastructure, we observed that SMS lure content, phishing URLs, vehicle registration numbers, and recipient phone numbers were repeatedly changing, indicating active operator-side campaign management rather than a static or abandoned database (see Figure 5). Similar eChallan-themed messages were also observed being received by users in the wild, further supporting the campaign's operational nature (see Figure 6). Figure 5 – Exposed SMS message configured to be sent to victims Figure 6 – Same SMSs are being received by the victims (Source – Twitter Post) One of the phishing URLs exposed through the GhostX infrastructure subsequently led us to a previously unseen GhostBat RAT variant, providing a direct investigative link among the backend control ecosystem, active phishing operations, and the malware's continued evolution. These findings led us to assess that GhostX is not a single Android malware family or standalone application. Instead, GhostX represents a broader operator-controlled ecosystem encompassing phishing infrastructure, backend services, Firebase-based configuration and command mechanisms, device-management functionality, and malware distribution. GhostBat RAT represents the Android implant operating within this ecosystem, with individual variants continuing to evolve across both delivery mechanisms and post-compromise capabilities. Technical Analysis Evolution of Droppers and Loaders GhostBat RAT has undergone continuous changes in its delivery and payload-protection mechanisms. Across the samples analyzed during the GhostX investigation, we identified multiple loader and dropper implementations designed to conceal the underlying malware payload, complicate static analysis, and reduce the effectiveness of hash- and signature-based detection. Although the recovered payloads demonstrate overlapping capabilities for surveillance, financial theft, and device control, the mechanisms used to deliver and recover them vary considerably across samples. Earlier variants relied on comparatively straightforward native loaders that decrypted embedded APK payloads using AES-CBC. Subsequent variants of Ghostbat RAT introduced XOR-encrypted custom containers, SPKZ/SPK1 packaging, split-APK delivery, dynamically loaded DEX components, and Java-based in-memory loaders. One variant moved away from embedded payload delivery entirely. It operated as a remote downloader, retrieving a second-stage APK from remote infrastructure, validating its SHA-256 hash, and installing it through Android's package installation framework. The most recent variant analyzed introduces a substantially more complex native loader implemented in libnetbridge.so. This loader combines multiple transformations, encryption, compression, and custom container stages before recovering the final GhostBat RAT payload. This diversification indicates continued modification of the delivery layer while broadly retaining the malware's post-compromise objectives. Consequently, detections that focus only on the outer APK, the encrypted asset name, or a single unpacking routine are unlikely to provide durable coverage. The GhostBat RAT loaders/droppers variants we observed are listed below: Figure 7 – GhostBat RAT Loader variants The most recent GhostBat RAT sample introduced a significantly more complex native unpacking mechanism. Unlike earlier variants that relied primarily on Java-based loaders or comparatively straightforward XOR/AES routines, this variant stores the encrypted payload inside an opaque application asset, assets/isti52q4, while most of the unpacking logic is implemented in the native library libnetbridge.so. The visible application code does not directly expose the final malicious functionality. Instead, execution transitions to the native loader, which processes the embedded asset through several sequential stages of transformation and decryption (see Figure 8). Figure 8 – Latest native dropper unpacking chain The first stage processes content within the encrypted asset file and derives values required for subsequent decoding. The resulting data is then passed through an RC4-like transformation before being processed through AES-256-GCM. This layered approach prevents the encrypted asset from being recovered using simple XOR or direct AES key extraction techniques that worked against earlier GhostBat RAT loaders. Following successful decryption, the loader recovers an MSZ1-formatted intermediate object that is decompressed using zlib. The decompressed data contains an MSP1 container that packages the final Android application components. The recovered payload consists of a split-APK application, including base.apk and split_config.dex.apk. The executable malware code is primarily contained within the recovered split configuration DEX. Unlike earlier samples, where the encrypted payload could be identified directly from ZIP headers or standard APK structures, the latest loader hides the final application behind several custom transformations before any recognizable Android package becomes available. This significantly increases the effort required for automated unpacking and reduces the effectiveness of simple asset-scanning techniques. Advanced GhostBat RAT Payload GhostBat RAT has evolved from an Android SMS and information stealer into a modular remote-access and Banking Trojan. Across the analyzed variants, the malware demonstrates capabilities for device profiling, SMS interception, remote SMS transmission, call-forwarding manipulation, payment-data theft, accessibility-based PIN capture, Firebase-driven command delivery, dynamic C&C configuration, and remote tunnelling. In the new GhostBat RAT variant, we observed the introduction of Android Accessibility Service abuse, a technique commonly associated with modern Android Banking Trojans. Earlier GhostBat RAT variants that we analyzed did not possess these capabilities during this investigation. The new variant uses Accessibility Service to monitor foreground applications, identify PIN-entry contexts, interact with application interfaces, and support two distinct credential-theft mechanisms: Ghost Overlay and targeted PIN/key-input capture. Once Accessibility Services access is granted, the malware monitors the foreground application and compares it against configured target lists. These targets can be managed through Firebase Remote Config, allowing operators to selectively activate credential-capture functionality when a targeted banking, UPI, wallet, or payment application is in use. Ghost Overlay The most notable capability introduced in this variant is the Ghost Overlay technique. Figure 9.1 – Ghost Overlay Attack Flow Unlike conventional Android overlay attacks that display a fake login or payment page over the legitimate application, GhostBat RAT does not need to replace the victim's banking interface. Instead, it places transparent accessibility overlay regions directly over the real PIN keypad displayed by the targeted application. The feature is controlled through Firebase Remote Config using: ghost_overlay_enabled ghost_overlay_packages Figure 9.2 – Ghost overlay initialization activity The default Ghost Overlay configuration targets the following Android packages: com.mobikwik_new com.google.android.apps.nbu.paisa com.google.android.apps.nbu.paisa.user Figure 10 – Target package list of Ghost Overlay activity When the malware detects one of these applications in the foreground and identifies a PIN-related activity, it creates a transparent keypad grid using Android’s TYPE_ACCESSIBILITY_OVERLAY. The overlay contains 12 touch regions matching the layout of a typical numeric PIN pad (see Figures 11 and 12): Figure 11 – Ghost PIN pad structure Figure 12 – Ghost overlay activity When the victim taps a digit on the legitimate Google Pay or MobiKwik PIN keypad, the transparent Ghost Overlay intercepts the touch event before it reaches the underlying application. The malware maps the touch coordinates to the corresponding keypad value and appends the resulting digit to an internal buffer used to reconstruct the PIN. To avoid interrupting the payment flow or alerting the victim, GhostBat RAT temporarily releases the affected overlay region and uses AccessibilityService.dispatchGesture() to reproduce the same tap at the corresponding screen coordinates (see Figure 13). As a result, the legitimate application receives the expected input and continues operating normally, while the malware records the victim's PIN in parallel. The same mechanism handles DEL and OK interactions, allowing the GhostBat RAT to update the captured digit sequence and detect when the PIN entry process has completed. This intercept-and-replay behavior enables the malware to observe PIN entry without presenting a fake Google Pay or MobiKwik interface. Figure 13 – dispatchGesture activity Once collected, the PIN is stored with metadata identifying the capture source as ghost_overlay and is subsequently queued for exfiltration over C&C “hxxps://api.cloudsettle[.]org/pin-data” (see Figure 14). Figure 14 – Storing captured Ghost PIN This technique is considerably stealthier than a conventional phishing overlay because the victim remains within the genuine financial application's interface throughout the interaction. GhostBat RAT effectively operates as an invisible intermediary, intercepting the victim's keypad interaction, recording the selected digits, and replaying those same touches into the legitimate application in near real time. Targeted Keylogging and PIN Capture In addition to the Ghost Overlay capability, the new GhostBat RAT variant implements a broader accessibility-based PIN/key-input capture mechanism targeting applications across India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital-payment ecosystem. Unlike the Ghost Overlay feature, which is specifically designed to intercept keypad touches in Google Pay and MobiKwik via transparent overlay regions, this functionality relies on Android Accessibility Service events to monitor user interactions across a much larger set of targeted applications. The default pin_target_packages configuration includes 60 Android package identifiers for financial applications used across India (see Figure 15). The target set includes applications associated with Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm, MobiKwik, BHIM, SBI UPI, Axis Pay, BharatPe, CRED, Freecharge, PayZapp, Groww, Navi, Jupiter, OneCard, JioFinance, Samsung Pay, and several other banking and payment services. The complete list of targeted Android packages is provided in the Targeted Application List section. Once Accessibility Service is granted, GhostBat RAT monitors foreground activity and determines whether the currently running application(s) match an entry in pin_target_packages. The malware then evaluates the surrounding application and screen context before treating observed numeric input as potentially sensitive PIN information. Figure 15 – PIN target package list The malware also uses configurable PIN-length boundaries, pin_min_digits, and pin_min_digits to determine whether the reconstructed numeric sequence is consistent with an expected PIN. Unlike Ghost Overlay, the broader keylogging mechanism does not rely on a transparent keypad overlay. Instead, GhostBat RAT uses Accessibility Service events and UI context to identify and reconstruct PIN-like input across a wider set of targeted financial applications, giving the malware substantially broader coverage within India’s banking and digital payment ecosystem. The analyzed variant contains a dedicated worker responsible for handling captured PIN information, “PinUploadWorker”. Captured PINS are locally queued before being transmitted to the endpoint “/pin-data”. Figure 16 – Captured PIN upload activity The introduction of this capability substantially expands the financial targeting of GhostBat RAT. Earlier variants primarily relied on SMS interception, OTP theft, phishing interfaces, and call-forwarding manipulation. The new variant can also monitor user interactions within legitimate financial applications and capture PIN-like input via Accessibility Service abuse. Command and Control Infrastructure The latest GhostBat RAT variant uses a multi-channel command-and-control architecture that combines a conventional HTTPS backend with Firebase services and a configurable WebSocket tunnel. Compared with earlier variants, which relied more heavily on hardcoded infrastructure, the new implementation provides greater operational flexibility by allowing the attacker to modify backend addresses and enable or disable selected malware capabilities remotely. In the analyzed sample, the default C&C infrastructure was configured as hxxps://api[.]cloudsettle[.]org. The malware communicates with this backend via multiple REST API endpoints that handle device registration, SMS collection, call log collection, command acknowledgement, PIN data submission, service state reporting, and other post-compromise functionality. Endpoint Purpose /sms/batch Uploads batches of SMS messages collected from the infected device /sms/new Sends newly received SMS messages to the C&C in near real time /sms/delivery-status Reports the delivery or failure status of remotely sent SMS messages /call-logs/batch Uploads collected call-log records in bulk /call-logs/new Sends newly observed call-log entries to the C&C /devices/sim-info Sends SIM and telephony-related information from the infected device /devices/update-token Registers or updates the device's Firebase Cloud Messaging token /devices/service-status Reports the operational status of malware services running on the device /commands/ack Acknowledges receipt or execution of commands issued by the C&C /commands/call-forward/status Reports the result or current state of call-forwarding operations /ping-response Responds to C&C ping requests and confirms that the infected device is online /upload-response Returns the result or status of generic upload or command operations /pin-data Uploads captured PIN-related data, including Ghost Overlay and broader PIN-capture records /live-keylog/status Reports or manages the operational state of the live keylogging functionality One of the major changes in the latest GhostBat RAT variant is the use of Firebase Remote Config as an additional control layer. The analyzed payload is associated with the Firebase project andromeda-d389d and retrieves remotely managed configuration values that control both infrastructure and malware functionality. Of particular interest is the base_url parameter, which allows the operator to replace the active REST backend without modifying or redistributing the APK. Therefore, api.cloudsettle.org represents the observed/default backend for this sample rather than a permanently fixed C&C address. Figure 17 – Dynamic C&C implementation A similar dynamic C&C approach was observed during the GhostX investigation. An earlier NextGen mParivahan sample associated with the ghostx-panel Firebase project retrieved its backend configuration from Firestore using the app_config/network document and the baseUrl field. In addition to the newly introduced Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay, targeted PIN capture, and dynamically configurable C&C functionality, GhostBat RAT continues to exhibit several core behaviors documented in our earlier research. These include collecting SMS messages from compromised devices, monitoring newly received messages for banking- and OTP-related content, stealing UPI credentials through fraudulent mParivahan payment interfaces, and registering compromised devices with attacker-controlled infrastructure. Earlier GhostBat RAT variants also used Telegram bots for device registration and operator notification, while selected dropper chains contained cryptocurrency-mining functionality alongside the information-stealing payload. These previously documented capabilities remain important to the overall GhostBat RAT operation; however, the latest variants significantly expand the malware's financial-theft and remote-control functionality. Rather than repeating the earlier functionality in detail, this analysis focuses on newly observed capabilities and architectural changes, particularly Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay PIN interception, broader targeting of financial applications, dynamic Firebase-based configuration, and evolving loader and C2 mechanisms. Conclusion The latest GhostBat RAT activity highlights continued evolution across both delivery mechanisms and post-compromise capabilities. The investigation into mParivahan- and eChallan-themed malware exposed the broader GhostX ecosystem, linking phishing infrastructure, backend control, and evolving GhostBat RAT payloads. The introduction of Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay, broader PIN capture, and Firebase-driven dynamic configuration significantly expands the malware’s financial-theft capabilities while making the operation more adaptable. Combined with continuously evolving loaders and active phishing activity, GhostBat RAT remains a threat to Android users, particularly across India’s banking, UPI, and digital payment ecosystem. Cyble’s Threat Intelligence Platforms continuously monitor emerging threats, infrastructure, and activity across the dark web , deep web , and open sources. This proactive intelligence empowers organizations with early detection, impersonation, infrastructure mapping, and attribution insights. Altogether, these capabilities provide a critical head start in mitigating and responding to evolving cyber threats . CRIL’s analysis of this campaign has been selected for the upcoming Association of Anti-Virus Asia Researchers (AVAR) conference, where these findings will be showcased. Our Recommendations We have listed essential cybersecurity best practices that form the first line of defense against attackers. We recommend that our readers follow the best practices given below: Install Apps Only from Trusted Sources: Download apps exclusively from official platforms like the Google Play Store . Avoid third-party app stores or links received via SMS, social media, or email. Be Cautious with Permissions and Installs: Never grant permissions and install an application unless you're certain of an app's legitimacy. Watch for Phishing Pages: Always verify the URL and avoid suspicious links and websites that ask for sensitive information. Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Use MFA for banking and financial apps to add an extra layer of protection, even if credentials are compromised. Report Suspicious Activity: If you suspect you've been targeted or infected, report the incident to your bank and local authorities immediately. If necessary, reset your credentials and perform a factory reset. Use Mobile Security Solutions: Install a mobile security application that includes real-time scanning. Keep Your Device Updated: Ensure your Android OS and apps are updated regularly. Security patches often address vulnerabilities that malware exploits. MITRE ATT&CK® Techniques Tactic Technique ID Procedure Initial Access Phishing (T1660) GhostBat RAT is distributed through smishing messages containing malicious links that redirect victims to fake mParivahan/eChallan or Google Play-style pages used to deliver the malicious APK. Persistence Event Triggered Execution: Broadcast Receivers (T1624.001) GhostBat RAT uses a boot-triggered Broadcast Receiver to restart its malicious services and workers after device reboot, allowing the implant to resume background activity. Defense Evasion Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location (T1655.001) GhostBat RAT masquerades as legitimate mParivahan/eChallan applications and uses government-themed names, icons, and interfaces to deceive victims. Defense Evasion Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing (T1406.002) GhostBat RAT uses multiple encrypted and packed loader mechanisms, including AES-CBC, XOR, SPKZ/SPK1, encrypted DEX stages, and the libnetbridge.so multi-stage loader to conceal the final payload. Defense Evasion Download New Code at Runtime (T1407) One observed GhostBat RAT delivery variant remotely downloads a second-stage APK, validates the payload, and installs it after the initial dropper executes. Defense Evasion Input Injection (T1516) GhostBat RAT abuses AccessibilityService.dispatchGesture() to replay intercepted PIN-keypad touches into legitimate Google Pay and MobiKwik applications as part of the Ghost Overlay technique. Credential Access Abuse Accessibility Features (T1453) The latest GhostBat RAT variant abuses Android Accessibility Service to monitor targeted financial applications, identify PIN-entry contexts, capture sensitive input, and support Ghost Overlay activity. Credential Access Input Capture: Keylogging (T1417.001) GhostBat RAT uses Accessibility Service events to capture PIN/key-input activity from targeted financial applications. The default configuration targets 60 Android banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and payment applications. Credential Access Input Capture: GUI Input Capture (T1417.002) Selected GhostBat RAT variants use fraudulent payment interfaces to capture UPI PINs, payment-card details, and other financial information entered by victims. Credential Access Access Notifications (T1517) Selected GhostBat RAT variants register a notification-listener service to monitor notifications generated by other applications, potentially exposing OTPs and other sensitive information. Discovery System Information Discovery (T1426) GhostBat RAT collects device information including Android version, device model, manufacturer, identifiers, and other system metadata. Discovery Software Discovery (T1418) GhostBat RAT can enumerate applications installed on the compromised device and uses package information to identify targeted banking and financial applications. Collection Protected User Data: SMS Messages (T1636.004) GhostBat RAT collects historical SMS messages and monitors newly received messages, including OTPs, banking alerts, and other sensitive message content. Collection Protected User Data: Call Log (T1636.002) GhostBat RAT collects call-history information and uploads historical and newly observed call-log records through its C2 infrastructure. Impact SMS Control (T1582) GhostBat RAT can receive attacker-defined SMS jobs and send messages through the infected device's SIM, allowing compromised devices to be used for remotely controlled SMS transmission and potentially further smishing activity. Impact Call Control (T1616) GhostBat RAT can manipulate and query call forwarding using USSD-based operations and report the forwarding state to its C2 infrastructure. Command and Control Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (T1437.001) GhostBat RAT communicates with its backend through HTTPS REST APIs and uses Firebase Cloud Messaging for command delivery. The latest variant also contains a configurable secure WebSocket communication channel.
